subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
That this House condemns the Government for its negligent and irresponsible approach to the protection and management of the environment, for its cuts of wildlife, meteorological and parks services, for abandoning Canada's past initiatives on the national and international levels to combat acid rain and to restore the water quality of the Great Lakes, and for thereby jeopardizing the health, economic well-being and the heritage of the present and future generations of Canadians.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the motion speaks for itself. We on this side of the House regret the performance of the Government on environmental matters and it has forced us to put forward today this motion of non-confidence.
As you may recall, Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) boasted about the long list of achievements on the part of his Government. He did not have the environment in mind, I am sure, otherwise he would not have indulged in self-congratulatory sentiments, as he did. We live, on the one hand, in a country where its citizens want the environment to be given priority, and this we have learned from public opinion polls. On the other hand, we have a Tory Government which pays lip service to the concerns about the environment which have been expressed by Canadians and delivers what, Mr. Speaker? What has this Government really delivered with respect to the environment in the past six months? That is the question.
Has this Government given the environment the high profile which Canadians expect? The answer, regretfully, is no. Has this Government created jobs in the environment? The answer, regretfully, is no. Actually, it has created unemployment through the cuts announced to the wildlife service and the National Research Council, through the interpretation centres, as well as other initiatives. Has the Government, through the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Blais-Grenier), met with the United States Environmental Protection Agency in order to discuss the quality of the water of the Niagara River and the Great Lakes? The answer, regretfully, is no. Has this Government strengthened the environmental protection measures which were developed since the inception of Environment
Canada in 1972 by successive Liberal Governments? And I would, of course, recognize with due respect a fine Minister for the environment, the present Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser). The Government has not strengthened the environmental protection measures which it inherited from the Liberal Government.
Has the Government strengthened the support Canada gives to finding a solution to global environmental issues? Here again, regretfully, the answer is no. Sadly enough, this Government has reduced Canada's contribution this year to the United Nations environmental program.
Has the Government celebrated Parks Canada's centennial by way of new park acquisitions or by way of a bold new program for its second centennial? The answer, regretfully, is no, certainly not. It has reduced Parks Canada's budget by $13 million.
Has the Government strengthened our future in renewable resources of energy so as to reduce our dependency on fossil fuels? Here again, regretfully, the answer is no, certainly not. It has disbanded the fine scientists and technicians working in this field at the National Research Council and increased the number of unemployed scientists and technicians in this country by wiping out the entire soft energy research unit in the NRC.
Has this Government accepted the plea by native people and fishermen along the Fraser River Valley who asked for a postponement of one year in the construction of double tracks proposed by Canadian National? The answer here, regretfully again, is no, certainly not. It has rejected their plea because this Government has not got the guts to act as it preaches.
Has this Government told the United States administration that we do have in Canada a program in place between 1980 and 1990 to reduce our sulphur dioxide emissions which contribute to acid rain by 25 per cent, and that parallel to that we have a unanimous commitment by federal and provincial environment Ministers to cut it by 50 per cent by 1994 by way of a plan for modernizing our non-ferrous industries? Certainly not, Mr. Speaker. This Government has neglected the unanimous federal, provincial and public support for these measures and actually thrown away our bargaining position, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) did last December, perhaps with a pathetic intention of currying favour with the Reagan administration.
Has this Government reached out, Mr. Speaker, to environmental groups and administrations? Has it sought their views before making these cuts, given them its long-term vision and generated a climate of confidence? Well, the answer here

again is no, certainly not. I am told there are many letters written last fall that are still to be answered. The morale among the non-governmental organizations and interested people is low. Their confidence in this Government is seriously damaged.
Well, Mr. Speaker, because of time limitations 1 have to stop here in this analysis, but we should ask ourselves at this point why is it that this Government is treating the environment in such a way despite last summer's promises? Is it because it does not understand the crucial importance of the relationship between the environment and the economy? Is it because it does not understand the crucial relationship between the environment and health? Is it because it understands the environment in isolation, like a luxury item? Is it because it sees the environment as a commodity which can be traded, sold, exploited at will? Is it because it is incapable of conceiving the environment as a common good which belongs to us all, be it water, air, soil, fish, all of which have to be managed carefully because we want to preserve it for future generations of Canadians? Is it because it is incapable of seeing and considering the environment as the foundation of our health and the foundation of our economy?
[DOT] (i1 IS)
There is evidently a conceptual deficiency on the part of the Government that makes me conclude that the future of the environment in the next few years looks very bleak indeed. Add to this the unfortunate fact that the Prime Minister has chosen as a Minister a person who gives the impression of considering the environment a bore, a nuisance one has to live with, rather than the exciting, meaningful and fascinating world that it is. It is a wonder consisting of the interaction of air, water, soil, flora and fauna, the coming together of living forces each with a role and a meaning from the amoeba to the sea lion, composing that wonderful and dynamic totality we commonly call nature.
We still have, thank God, a terrific Department called Environment Canada to which my colleagues and I would like to pay tribute today. It consists of fine and dedicated civil servants, men and women committed to the well-being of our economy and our health through a sound management of the environment. The only problem with Environment Canada today is the poor judgment of the Prime Minister when he appointed the present Minister, and his insensitivity to the necessity of correcting his mistake. Every day that goes by without bringing in a new Minister, the Prime Minister demonstrates his lack of commitment to the promises he made during the election to environmental groups and Canadians at large. What a sham!
The Prime Minister bears the main responsibility for the fact that the state of the environment has deteriorated in the past six months. He has chosen the wrong person as Minister. He has downgraded Canada's role at home and abroad in combating acid rain, an issue which is so close to the hearts of Canadians. He has given away Canada's bargaining position with the U.S. administration. He also bears the responsibility
for sending out the wrong signals by allowing cuts in the industrial and regional development fund where the dollars are to be found for the modernization of our non-ferrous smelters.
The Minister of the Environment has allowed cuts in the environment programs of the Canadian Wildlife Service and the interpretation centres, without consulting the provinces, despite the promises made in the Speech from the Throne, and without consulting interested organizations. The Minister has failed in the important role of building bridges with non-governmental groups and environmentally interested individuals. They are reporting that they feel abandoned by the Government. The Minister has not yet addressed the crucial and complex issue of water, particularly in the Great Lakes. She has yet to meet with the Environmental Protection Agency in the United States.
So far the Minister of the Environment has not made a speech of substance for the public record, except for replies in the House and one ceremonial speech last week. There has been no intellectual, political contribution on her part to the environmental issues of our times. There has been not one ounce of contribution to issues such as South Moresby and Meares Islands, which are sensitive issues for millions of Canadians today who want these areas preserved for future generations. There has not been one ounce of contribution, intellectually or otherwise, to water quality and quantity and what water means to future generations of Canadians.
There has not been one ounce of contribution on the issue of herbicides and pesticides as they are used in agriculture and forestry today, and the search for alternatives. There has not been one ounce of contribution on the long-term but important issue of the greenhouse effect on our climate. There has not been one ounce of contribution on the issue of nuclear winter, which is the ultimate environmental issue. There has been no contribution on issues between the environment and health and the environment and our economy, which is based on natural resources and therefore must rely on a properly managed environment. There has not been one ounce of contribution to the Canada Parks centennial and the future of parks extensions, with respect to the future of the North and the great potential there for parks before the land is locked up.
There has not been one ounce of contribution with respect to whether Lancaster Sound should be used for tanker routes. There has not been any contribution on Canada's role in UNEA and our global role in the environment to sustain the fine reputation that we as a Government, as a nation and as Canadians have earned over the last decade.
Last week in the House, the Minister of the Environment gave no visible support for her colleagues, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie), who were visibly distressed in their efforts to postpone the CN double tracking in the Fraser River Valley for one year, as recommended unanimously by the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry.

March 5, 1985

In conclusion, in this litany of misery our country is without a Minister of the Environment. At best, it has a phantom or a Minister that never was.
The Prime Minister has not backed up his words with action. While he has been great on public relations, he has done nothing of substance so far with respect to the environment. He has shown poor judgment by appointing the present Minister of the Environment. He has given away the store in our bilateral relations with the United States on acid rain that are coming up this month in Quebec. Not only has he disappointed them, he has angered Canadians from coast to coast. Therefore, we have moved our motion of non-confidence because the record of the Tory Government over the past six months is simply a sham.

First, Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate my colleague from Davenport (Mr. Caccia) on an interesting and extremely relevant speech.
Here is my question: Earlier this morning the media reported that the United States will tighten up controls on leaded gas emissions in an attempt to eliminate lead from gas by 1988. As former Minister and our party's critic in environmental matters, could the Hon. Member tell us what he thinks of that objective and what measures Canada might take to do away with leaded gas in the not too distant future?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for his question. Speaking for myself, and I am at one with everybody else on this issue, I heartily welcome the decision made by the American Environmental Protection Agency. That decision will go a long way towards reducing gasoline lead content to what may be the lowest level worldwide. And what did we do in 1983? We took the necessary steps to match the American performance by 1986 with respect to leaded gas. Last May, when the American Government announced its intention to reduce gas lead content further still, I strongly supported this initiative and I hope that the commission mandated by the previous Liberal administration to set future target levels after 1986 will draw inspiration from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's latest decision. It means that, in two stages, we might reduce gas lead content to the same level as the Americans, perhaps later even though our common goal is to protect our children's health.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am a little concerned about this matter of removing lead from gasoline. Does the Hon. Member realize that there are thousands of farm machines in this country that were made to use leaded gasoline? If we ever get to the point where all lead is removed from gasoline, there will be a monetary burden on the shoulders of our agricultural community. Those machines are there. They should be good for 10 or 12 years. We should not simply nullify the investment of our farmers and ignore the fact that they need lead in gasoline to operate their equipment. I am a little concerned when I hear people saying that we will remove all lead from gasoline by a certain date. We should have some consideration for those people who bought machines which can only be fueled with leaded gasoline. I should like to have the Hon. Member's comments.

speakeroldname: Hon. Suzanne Blais-Grenier (Minister of the Environment):
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity today to recall what has been done by this Government and my Department since we came to power.
The Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) has taken his Party's usual somber, dramatic and strident approach in having us believe that this country is at death's door. Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is setting himself up as the saviour of humanity, of Canada, of wildlife, of the health of Canadians, and as an expert on acid rain and hazardous products. He knows the pressure groups, which are friends of his, and he is going to tell us he would have done a much better job.
Mr. Speaker, we in the Progressive Conservative Party have always been very clear in our choice of words. We said that we were here to undo the harm done by the previous Government's extravagant spending, a Government that made us live on credit for 15 years and which emptied the coffers of all the departments before we came to power. I have some examples in my own Department, of contracts that were signed between September 4 and September 17. There was a rush to empty the Treasury, and since that time they have been complaining loud and clear because the present Government has been obliged to make cutbacks. However, Canadians have realized it was time the Government stopped living on credit. Canadians have a lot of sense-a lot more than the Hon. Member for Davenport.
Mr. Speaker, I am very proud of what I have accomplished in my Department, and despite all the somber remarks by my colleague, I can inform the House that after my swearing in, I was in my office at 8:30 the next morning, having talks with my officials. Two weeks later, I met Canadian Environment Ministers at a federal-provincial conference in Newfoundland, and I asked their support for the major plans and priorities I was setting up for the Department. Unlike the Liberals, however, I did not feel obliged to tell any reporter who wanted to listen what I was going to do in the months to come. All these decisions will be announced in due time. Mr. Speaker, I therefore met with the Ministers of the Environment who were assembled in Newfoundland, and we set up a common action plan to deal with the most pressing problems confronting Canada's environment. Unlike the former Government, we sat down together, we developed strategies, we talked, we understood each other and we shared responsibilities. Can the Hon. Member for Davenport say as much, after he told people on American television, and I shall quote him in his own language so he will understand me clearly:

Keep your garbage in your own country.
March 5, 1985

That, Mr. Speaker, is typical of the attitude of the previous Government which is criticizing us today for taking the time to sit down with representatives of our clients, for taking the time to consult and to reach an understanding with the provinces instead of getting carried away by all kinds of action plans that are totally useless. In fact, the only thing my hon. colleague produced during his mandate as Minister is a lot of grand statements. In this Government, we do not make grand statements, Mr. Speaker. We act.
At the beginning of October, I met with my federal and provincial colleagues and we sat down to set up a strategy. At the end of October, with my colleague, the Minister for External Affairs, I signed the Skagit Agreement between British Columbia and the State of Washington. This agreement has been in the works for 42 years. Mr. Speaker, that is one accomplishment. After only six weeks, a Minister is still new to the job, but this Minister, after six weeks, signed an agreement that had been in the works for 42 years. Because it had not been feasible to conclude the agreement, Mr. Speaker? Not at all! Because the previous Government did not feel like helping the provinces solve their problems.
Finally, in October I met with the Habitat Foundation and shed some of the responsibilities of my Department, entrusting them to a private organization which has since made tremendous progress at a far lower cost than would have been the case if it had been the federal Government. I can also assure you that I have frequent and entirely cordial consultations with the Habitat Foundation.
In early December, I met with representatives of Canadian steel mills. They told me it was the first time a Minister of the Environment spoke to them and sat down with them to try and assess their problems. It was the first time a Minister said: Let us solve the acid rain problem together!
I have also met with representatives from the mining and chemical industries to discuss the control of hazardous and toxic products. Furthermore, I went to London to prepare for the Economic Summit. With my Environment colleagues, we got together to try and set up and prepare the subject matter that will be discussed by the Prime Ministers and representatives of the countries taking part in the Bonn Economic Summit in May.
And that is not all. While my colleague spent days with newspaper reporters telling them that I was unable to perform as a Minister, I was setting up a federal-provincial conference-again with the Ministers of Environment-to hammer out an agreement on acid rains. Throughout Canada, this has been hailed as a historical agreement which, for the first time, will enable the provinces and the federal Government to set their own acid rain reduction standards. That is what we have accomplished in six months, not to mention some other things.

In January, for instance, I was in Toronto to attend a meeting of wildlife Ministers, the first time ever for a federal Minister.
Well, as my colleague points out, here is someone who does not understand Canada's wildlife problems, who could not care less and who supports the Department of Environment as something that must be supported since there is no other option.
Mr. Speaker, I would suggest that the rhetoric of my colleague on the other side of the House no longer fools Canadians. That is why they voted for an open Government on September 4, a Government which has little use for empty talk but which takes action and tells them: We do have problems in this country. We are overburdened by the deficit, but we will pull through by working together. That is the kind of language they have not heard in 22 years, Mr. Speaker.
It was with all those considerations in mind that I took over the Department of Environment and targeted five major priorities during my term in office. That is more than my colleague has ever done.
Within and without Canada, I stress the fact that an unpolluted environment is the prerequisite of economic growth. That is why I convened for March 11 a conference on environmental and economic issues where environment specialists and businessmen will sit at the same table for the first time in an attempt to solve problems rather than create conflicts by distorting situations beyond recognition.
Mr. Speaker, that national consultation on the economy ought to broaden future perspectives and is our response to Canadians who have told us in a recent poll that they are quite prepared to reach for their wallet if that will help solve environmental problems. According to the poll, most of them would readily contribute between $5 and $15 per capita to come to grips with what everyone knows are very complicated problems.
During the same time, Mr. Speaker, I cut departmental staff by some 405 person-years, but no one has ever mentioned the 6,000 public service jobs eliminated by the Liberal Government between 1979 and 1981. But they did try to turn those 400 person-years into an issue, making quite a fuss about it and claiming that Canada's environment and wildlife were in dire straits. What about those 405 person-years which represent about 300 public servants? The number is steadily going down. Here is the situation: All positions have been filled, except for 35 to 40. That is what my Opposition colleague and some newspapermen following his trail kept repeating throughout the fall to describe what they termed the dangerous situation of wildlife in Canada.
The Department still has several thousand employees and a budget of $800 million. I think that Canadians are in favour of our withdrawing as much as possible from very costly programs which can be taken over by volunteers and innovative

private sector interests, and I suggest that the Wildlife Habitat Foundation is the best example of that.
My colleague claims that I have shown no concern for water resources, Mr. Speaker. We did show concern for water resources and settled some outstanding issues about five weeks ago. We renewed the water agreement with Ontario, we looked into the situation of the Great Lakes and we are now busy setting up monitoring facilities. 1 have had several conversations with the Chairman of the commission of inquiry on water management in Canada and we are looking forward to receiving his report and recommendations in the near future. I can assure my colleague that I will implement the Pearse report recommendations to the extent permissible by my departmental resources. The Chairman of the Pearse Commission is already quite pleased with our support and the discussion I had with him.
We want to cooperate with the people instead of taking unilateral decisions in our Ottawa ivory tower. Consultation does take time and I intend to take all the time necessary to make the process work. I will unveil very important decisions in the next few days and I am convinced that the Canadian public is quite satisfied with the Government at this time. Canadians realize that 22 years of inertia in federal departments cannot be eradicated overnight, that it will take some time. The economy must be handled very rationally and very carefully, and the Canadian public is certainly not complaining, unlike our hon. friends opposite. In poll after poll, Canadians have shown they are happy to see a Conservative Government of our caliber leading the country.
They say I have done nothing about acid rain. Might I remind the House of the Montreal agreement with the provinces and the action plan we promised and which is still being pursued. That is one of the promises we made during the election campaign. We are preparing for the Bonn Summit. An agreement is to be signed with Sweden in early April and another agreement under the auspices of CITES in Brazil at the end of April, and at the OECD in June, and all these decisions require a tremendous amount of research and planning. When people complain that I am hiding in my office, Mr. Speaker, I am indeed in my office, but I am preparing strategies for action and discussing problems with my colleagues and making decisions, and obviously, I do not spend my time sitting at the door of the Press Club on Wellington Street. Besides, it is a bit cool for that sort of thing these days, although I might consider doing so next June.
I make a habit of working in my office with my departmental officials and not announcing decisions until they have been finalized and can be made public. I am very happy and proud to be Minister of the Environment, and I promise my hon. friend opposite that my mandate at Environment will be a very fruitful one and that it will not compare in any way with his own mandate.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I certainly would not want to put words in the Minister's mouth, as she suggested. In Tory language, how many people lost their jobs as a result of the Minister's cuts?

Mr. Speaker, I am beginning to learn the meaning of the word "hysteria". I would like to thank the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) for giving us the opportunity to debate the approach of this Government to the protection and management of the environment. If there is one area where this Government has clearly failed, where it has clearly stumbled since its election, it is in the area of the environment.
The Government has failed in two ways, Mr. Speaker. First, it is doing things which it does not have a mandate to do. At no time during the election campaign did the Government indicate it would take the attitude it is now taking towards the environment. Second, the Government is making many mistakes in what it is doing and these will come back to haunt us for years to come.
I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Blais-Grenier) sees fit to leave the House in the midst of a debate on the environment.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) rises on a point of order to say, I presume, that the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) should not allude to the fact that the Minister has left the House. I believe the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill knows that.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
The fact remains, Mr. Speaker, that this is further evidence of a continuing unwillingness on the part of the Minister, with the exception of the one time she appeared before the committee on December 20, to engage in a dialogue, either with Members of Parliament or with the public, as to the advisability of the cuts she has made.
As I said before, Mr. Speaker, this Government has failed and stumbled with respect to the environment and I would like to go over a few of those areas. The first area has to do with
the cuts to the Canadian Wildlife Service. In the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry to which the Department of the Environment reports, we have heard testimony after testimony, evidence after evidence and witness after witness to the effect that the cut-backs which were made by the Minister to the Canadian Wildlife Service are a very serious error and will damage not only the environment but the ability of the Canadian Government to manage the environment by causing itself to lose the expertise of so many people.
Rather than quoting over and over again what witnesses have had to say in front of the committee, Mr. Speaker, I would just like to call the attention of the House to an article in the magazine Equinox for March-April, 1985, which I just received yesterday. It is entitled "What Price Wildlife?" The sub-title reads: "Venerated at Home, Respected Abroad, the Canadian Wildlife Service becomes an endangered species". I commend this article to those Hon. Members in the House and to those of the public who may be interested in the effect of the cut-backs to the Canadian Wildlife Service.
Even though I have been paying attention to the issue, obviously, as the environment critic for my Party, I hadn't quite realized just how ridiculous and absurdly stupid some of these cuts are until I had the opportunity to read this article, which pointed out the full human and environmental dimensions of some of the work which was going on. I will not say much more about the Canadian Wildlife Service cut-backs except to quote the last paragraph of this article, which I think puts it extremely well. It paraphrases what Tony Keith, a biologist in the Canadian Wildlife Service, has to say:
What Keith is saying is that sooner or later, some prairie slough will fill with the floating carcasses of ducks, killed by untested chemicals from a cropduster that accidentally overflew a field. Anthrax and brucellosis will cause bison to totter and fall to the muskegs of northern Alberta, and there will be no wildlife veterinarian to treat them. National park wardens may even come across the bloodied body of a camper, the victim of a grizzly attack that might have been prevented with another season's research into bears' feeding habits. And the public outcry may then be so loud that the politicians who are today making the cuts will be forced to rehire the very biological expertise they now dismiss as surplus to departmental requirements. Canadians will have learned the hard way about the true costs of casting out decades of accumulated ecological knowledge for the sake of quick-fix adjustments to one year's federal budget.
That is the kind of short-sightedness, Mr. Speaker, which these cuts represent. It is the kind of short-sightedness which I am still hopeful will be condemned by the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry itself. That committee has shown some leadership in this House by unanimously recommending to the House some time ago that the double-tracking of the CNR in the Ashcroft subdivision be put on hold because of the environmental consequences as well as the question of the well-being of the native people. I am hoping that that committee will show the same kind of leadership with respect to the cut-backs to the Canadian Wildlife Service. No one has come before the committee to say a good word about the cuts and any committee worth its salt, after it has heard this unanimous evidence, must then say itself that these cuts ought to be reserved by the Minister, and soon, because many of them are about to take place.
March 5, 1985

What else has the Government done with respect to the environment? It has already been noted that it cut back on its contribution to the United Nations environment program, which was embarrassing internationally. It is just further evidence of the way in which this Government is falling into line behind the United States and its attitude toward UN programs. The Minister of the Environment celebrates the hundredth anniversary of national parks in Canada by going ahead with a $13 million cut to our national parks and by rambling on about the privatization of them.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that I first raised the issue of the further $13 million cut in this House just before Christmas and no one paid much attention then. But we see the cut-back coming now to our national parks. That is the way the Conservatives celebrate the centenary of our national parks, and it is now talking about privatization. Is there not a Tory in the crowd, an Hon. Member sitting opposite, who knows that at the very least our parks are public? We can argue about other areas of economic activity but I thought we had come to the point where we did not have to talk about whether parks should be privatized or not. Yet that is the sort of ideological silliness and extremeness which we find on the part of certain Hon. Members opposite, and the Minister of the Environment in particular.
What has the Government done with respect to renewable energy and the environmental benefits of developing that energy option as opposed to many of the other options which we have concentrated on for so many years? It almost wiped that option out completely while going ahead with the uncritical attitude towards the nuclear option which was so characteristic of the previous Liberal Government.
What has the Government done with respect to doubletracking and the recommendation of the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry and, by the way, the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development, with respect to that action? We still have no assurances as yet that that double-tracking will not go ahead until all of the concerns of the native people, the fishermen and the people who are concerned about the salmon habitat have been met. In fact, we witnessed a debate last week in which a Conservative majority on the other side of the House prevented a vote from taking place and prevented a debate from being extended. I must say at the same time that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser) and the chairman of the committee abstained from that obstruction, and that is to their credit. There we had one afternoon where Parliament almost seemed to be working. It almost seemed as if some independence was going to be exerted by Parliament and its committees over the Government with respect to this important environmental issue. But where was the Minister of the Environment? She was not even around for that.
Another environmental failure by this Government was the decision taken with respect to the herbicide Allachlor and the way in which the Department of Agriculture has been allowed
Supply
to continue the policy established over the Liberal decades of letting the users, that is to say Agriculture and Transport, have the final say over what is used instead of the people who are making recommendations from a health or environmental point of view, being the Department of National Health and Welfare and the Department of the Environment. That is a question of structure and the low priority given to environmental concerns in the bureaucracy or the hierarchy of ministries, if you like. This has to change if we are to be able to address some of these issues. I had hoped we might be able to see some of that change if we had a strong Minister of the Environment. Instead, we have hardly a Minister at all. So I am not very hopeful on that score.
With respect to Canada-U.S. relations and the whole question of acid rain, Great Lakes water quality and so on, what have we seen? We have the Shamrock Summit coming and we still have not seen any action by this Government with respect to an announcement that it will move to reduce auto emissions to the standard pertaining in the United States. Are we going to get that announcement before March 17? That would have been something the Minister could have talked about. We still do not know. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), instead of having to make a private telephone call to Mr. Reagan as the paper reported this morning, then might have something to show. He might be able to say that we have come up to scratch with respect to auto emission standards and now we expect them to come across. We then would not be in the position of having to acquiesce to the argument that I am sure the President will make, as he has done time and time again, about the need for more research.
The United States has really not accepted that this is a problem. As an article by David Suzuki in The Toronto Star on Saturday says, Mr. Speaker, the demand for absolute proof is a polluter's cop-out excuse. That is exactly what is going on with respect to acid rain in the U.S. That is why I welcomed the Prime Minister's remarks some months ago about having to go to the bargaining table with clean hands. If that was not just sort of a preliminary for not doing anything, then we need to see some action to indicate the Prime Minister was serious. One of the ways he could show us he was serious would be by making an announcement about nitrous oxide before March 17.
We could have full reinstatement of the herring gull program instead of one out of six people in the program being reinstated. That would be a sign that we were serious about at least monitoring Great Lakes water quality, if not doing anything about it. But instead the Minister announced that she was reinstating the program, and a month or two later we find out that one person out of six has been reinstated. That work is not being done.

speechtext: It is called fraud.

speechtext:
I agree. It was a fraudulent announcement, meant to mislead people and take the heat off the Minister for a little while. Maybe it did in an insignificant way, but people have come to know that the program has not been reinstated.

March 5, 1985

But that is one of the things the Minister could do and which the Prime Minister could do if he wanted to sit down with clean hands at the bargaining table on March 17.
Again with respect to the herring gull program, we see an article on the front page of The Globe and Mail yesterday about the inadequate registry of birth defects we have in this country. That is something, of course, that we cannot immediately dump on the lap of the present Government. That inadequacy belongs to previous Liberal Governments. But if the Government was serious about trying to move in that environmental area, it would take steps to make adequate its registry of birth defects. It would take steps to make adequate environmental monitoring programs like the herring gull program and then we could have some confidence. Part of the problem is that you listen to the Minister but you never get one squeak of passion about the environment. Not so much as a murmur or a moan. Nothing. You would hardly even know she was the Minister of the Environment. She could at least have the decency to get up and sound as if she regrets the fact she had to make these cuts. But you do not even get a sense that she regrets it. That is the thing that causes us real despair. If the Minister could get up and say this is the burden of necessity and she wished she did not have to do it, that is one thing. But instead she gets up and talks the fiscal language game and implies these programs are extravagant, redundant, a luxury which can be sacrificed. This is what causes despair as much as the cuts themselves. The Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) says the Minister is Canada's answer to James Watt. I am afraid that is so true.
The Americans do not have any problem standing up for their interests. They are trying to put the heat on President Reagan now to take a message to Prime Minister Mulroney concerning our laws on generic drugs. Why can our Prime Minister not take the same kind of firm message to the United States at the Shamrock Summit?
I am not just sure how much time I have left, Mr. Speaker, but I have a few more things I want to comment on and then I would like to move an amendment. I would like to spend a little more time on acid rain because this is a question of maturity, of how we relate to the U.S. As I said before, the U.S. does not have any problems sticking up for itself. We just had an experience in Manitoba where, because Manitoba and Canada and the people were firm on the Garrison River diversion project, the North Dakotans are saying that they are going to prohibit the import of Canadian electricity. I guess that is what you call a mature response!
That is the kind of mature relationship that the Minister wants with the United States. Or is it, of course, because I say that with tongue in cheek? On the other hand, a Bill has been introduced in Congress saying that if Canada does not clean up its act on acid rain, they are going to ban imports of Canadian electricity. So on the one hand we are getting it because we are environmentally sensitive, and on the other hand we are going to get the same penalty for not being environmentally sensitive. So sometimes our neighbours to the South do act irrationally. What I am saying is that if the
Prime Minister is serious about having a mature relationship with the U.S., then he needs to go to that table, hopefully with clean hands, and then he will be able to be firm with the President over acid rain and other issues.
I mentioned before the question of renewable resources and the need to develop them and the fact that funding for them has been wiped out. But they never were given a very high priority when you compare the hundreds of millions of dollars which have been poured down the drain in the nuclear industry in this country as a result of technological vanity and the refusal to criticize that industry, which was so characteristic of the previous Liberal regime.
I have an amendment which I think would add a great deal to this motion and would put the environmental picture more in balance if it were to be accepted by the House. Therefore I move, Mr. Speaker, seconded by the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton), that after the words "Great Lakes" the following words be added:
-for continuing the long established bias toward the environmentally dangerous option of nuclear power over alternative and renewable energy sources,
If I have any time left, Mr. Speaker, I will speak to the amendment.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, perhaps I could say a word about the issue of nuclear power versus other sources of energy. To myself and a lot of Canadians who are concerned about the environment, this is the central or paradigmatic question. How you view the role of nuclear power determines your understanding of environmental issues. As long as we continue to pour inordinate amounts of money into that particular energy option while we spend trifling amounts or nothing at all, as will be the case under this Government, on renewable energy sources, we are committed to a technological world view that ultimately will be destructive of the environment which we all say we care about. That is why this amendment is important and why we ought to debate it.

speechtext:

I suggest he might want to visit the Prairies.
The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill is from the west. Does he think that the Department of the Environment and

the Minister of the Environment, because of a health hazard problem in Toronto or Montreal, should put forward regulations which govern farming on the Prairies? speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill does not have to answer the question because I believe it relates to the speech of the Hon. Member for Davenport. However, if he wishes, he may.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I understood the second half of the question to be directed to me. I would like to take issue with the view expressed by the Hon. Member that it was the Liberal way to have the Department of National Health and Welfare make a recommendation and then apply it uncritically right across the country. In fact, the Liberal record is that the Department of National Health and Welfare did not have much say at all. It made lots of recommendations, most of which were not heeded. I do not think the Hon. Member was paying attention all those years while he was watching the Liberal Government. If he had been paying attention he would have seen that it was as I said it was. The Departments of National Health and Welfare and the Environment did not have much clout. It was the Departments of Agriculture and Transport which made the decisions. The quality of those decisions, and whether those decisions with respect to health hazards ought to take into account certain realities, is another matter. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought the Member made an excellent speech. Because of the pressures of time there were two items which he did not deal with at any length. He did not really talk about the Liberal record in this area. We must recognize that the problems we are facing at this time are not new. These problems did not occur after September 4. Acid rain, the lack of progress in negotiations with the United States, and the problems we face in so many fields, are a result of many years of Liberal Government. We must remember that it failed to protect the environment. I would like to hear the comments of the Member on that.
The other item which I think is important and which has become public recently is that the Atomic Energy Control Board has completely failed to control and regulate the nuclear industry in the country. There is information that workers have been forced to inhale radiodactive dust, that radioactive materials have been left in towns because there is lack of adequate storage, and that the Atomic Energy Control Board refused to listen to its own research staff when making its decisions. I have called for an inquiry into the role of the Atomic Energy Control Board and the nuclear industry in the country. I would like to hear the Member's view on that.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the first point the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) made is a good one, but I would
Supply
like to spend most of my time on the second point with respect to the nuclear industry. Over the years the Liberal Government had a totally uncritical commitment to the nuclear industry and the nuclear option. Any attempts to have a critical review conducted ended up in an internal departmental review. There were no public hearings or public discussions on what was involved in a continuing commitment to this option.
The Conservatives were different in 1979. One of the first things they announced in 1979 was a parliamentary inquiry into the nuclear fuel cycle. What happened to that, Mr. Speaker? All we get now is an odd statement from the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) about the possible commercial benefits of nuclear power or, even more frightening, ramblings from the same Minister about the commercial benefits of Canada becoming a radioactive garbage dump for the rest of the world. I can show you the comments of the Minister in a letter to the town council of Gimli in that respect, Mr. Speaker.
The Government has a totally commercial view of the nuclear industry. That means that we will not get an inquiry or debate. Canadians will not be invited to talk about the kind of energy future they want. It will be full speed ahead, business as usual, just like the Liberals when it comes to nuclear energy. That is very unfortunate, Mr. Speaker.
The Hon. Member for Davenport asked me a question informally and I would like to put it on the record. He asked, "What about uranium mining in Saskatchewan?" In this House in 1980 I stood up in the course of a debate on a Private Member's Bill of mine calling for a moratorium on nuclear power and said that I was against uranium mining in Saskatchewan, no matter who mines it and no matter who happens to be in power. I still take that position. Fortunately, that is now the position of the Saskatchewan and the federal New Democratic Party. There is complete unanimity within the Party with respect to uranium mining and the need to phase it out.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it bothers me that the Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) on the one hand asks the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Blais-Grenier) why she is cutting research. On the other hand, when he talks about the President of the United States, he says he wants research. Is the Member for research or against research in the environment?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that is about the dumbest question I have been asked in a long time, but I will try to answer it. We do not need more research on acid rain. We know we have a problem and we must act. We must continue research on the consequences of pesticides in sloughs in prairie Canada or other things which are working their way into our environment, because we must learn how to act. The only straw man that the Member sets up is himself.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I made it quite clear that I think all of the cuts to the Canadian Wildlife Service should be cancelled. However, the Hon. Member and his Government has not given us an honest answer yet with respect to the other side of the spending question concerning tax expenditures. When the Government comes clean as to the S30 billion to $50 billion that it is spending in the form of tax expenditures, we will be able to get an accurate picture of what is happening. At that time we will know all of the ways in which the public treasury is being drained of money, not only through spending on programs but through spending in the form of revenue that is never collected. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to continue debate and try to deal with some of the questions that have been raised. It is my opinion that some of these issues which have been introduced into debate are red herrings. I am accustomed to hearing debate from the Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) and the Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) and have been impressed by their generosity, understanding and sincerity. However, in the last two or three months it has been difficult to maintain that impression due to their inability to understand and apply constructive criticism to the Government's efforts on behalf of the environment.
March 5, 1985

Let there be no mistake that our Government intends to provide the action that is needed in order to ensure that our environmental scene will benefit all Canadians and protect our future heritage.
The Hon. Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Blais-Grenier) wishes to apologize to the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill for being unable to listen to his comments. She had other obligations which required her to be elsewhere and it was difficult for her to rearrange her schedule because the motion was introduced as late as possible yesterday. However, she will read the Hon. Member's speech in Hansard.
Let me try to explain the position of both Opposition Parties with respect to environmental issues, as I understand it. On November 8, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) gave the clearest indication ever of the conditions under which the Government must operate. We opened the books as much as possible to explain the economic situation we faced. Many of the departments did their best to reduce their expenditures in the short time they were given. This included the Department of the Environment which, after considering its full range of programs, had to decide which programs could appropriately and reasonably be cut back.
In spite of the positive advances that we have made which I believe all Canadians support, Members opposite have for some unexplained reason decided to approach this issue on a personal basis, as is evident from the comments made by the Member for Davenport. I think they have lost sight of the objectives and requirements with respect to the environment of Canada.
One of our first steps, even as an Opposition Party, was to support a new park for Canada in this centennial year of Parks Canada. The Minister stated as recently as several weeks ago that under the Conservative Government and her Department there is a definite and increasing future for national parks in Canada. I cannot guarantee that it would be established on the exact terms of reference with which all Members would be completely content but that commitment has been made and I believe it will be honoured.
The background alluded to by one of the questioners of the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill, the background to this whole situation with the environment, is one that cannot be discussed without ascribing some responsibility, particularly to the Member for Davenport. If there is one piece of testimony that says it all and one that should not be viewed as politically partisan, it would have to be a document that was produced and released at the end of last year called "Time Lost". The committee was chaired by the former Member for Sault Ste. Marie. Members from all Parties served on that committee. There were those who distinguished themselves, such as the Hon. Member for Vancouver South, the Minister for Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser), and the Hon. Member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling), who is well known to all people concerned, especially on the acid rain issue. What this committee which had been reconstituted from 1980 to 1984
Supply
found was that there had not been any accomplishment. The Minister in the previous Government had really not been able to accomplish anything, although he had brave words, passionate statements and press releases almost every day from his Department. But if you come right down to the nitty-gritty, Mr. Speaker, what he really ended up with was an empty hand. He was not able to produce. It may not have been all his fault. It may have been the disposition of people with whom he had to work in the Cabinet, and for that I can only offer him my sympathy.

Commitments have been made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). I believe statements made in the past few weeks by the Prime Minister repeated very clearly and soundly that we intend to fulfil our commitments. He has recognized the difficulty in dealing honestly and effectively with the President of the United States and in accomplishing the needs that we have on our own domestic scene to reduce the terrible environmental burden of continuous air pollution, particularly as a result of acid rain.
The Hon. Member has asked about auto emissions. In contrast to what occurred before, there were hearings which took place in 1984 which brought all of the interested parties, all of those affected and concerned, together to consider all of the specifics that one must consider when one talks about controlling auto emissions. We have a very bad record in the control of auto emissions. I do not think the previous Minister who was criticizing us today has much room, if he is honest with himself, for standing in the House and affronting the Minister of the Environment after three or four months, a period that has been filled almost continuously with consultation and efforts to address in a serious way the problems we have to face. The commitment has been made for action, Mr. Speaker. We will be judged on the basis of whether we can produce that action.
The background for this debate is also around the centennial year for Parks Canada. Parks Canada started out 100 years ago with several individual Canadians, actually two people, who did not like what was happening. I think the CN was involved at that time.

Excuse me, I apologize, it was the CP.
The interesting point, and the point that I raise now, is that this is a reflection of something we need to get back to. It is one of the things that this Government and this Minister has

March 5, 1985
Supply
been trying to do and which will be shown in the future to be very effective. It is to listen and to work with individual Canadians, be it private enterprise on an individual basis with voluntary organizations or whatever, to try to develop, protect and maintain environmental standards and conditions in the best interests of all Canadians.
The most specific and recent example is the Creston Valley Wildlife Interpretive Centre. During the budget cuts announced on November 8, it is clear that the Wildlife interpretive Centres, five of them across Canada, face closure. In working with a local group in British Columbia, that particular interpretive centre will now remain open and will continue to remain open partially with support of the provincial Government and the Minister of the Environment of British Columbia, Environment Canada and the Minister of the Environment, and private voluntary groups. That is an example we hope will be repeated, perhaps not in exactly the same way but in a similar way in Wye Marsh. This is an example that can be repeated right across Canada.
In the same vein, hearing the criticisms of the wildlife cuts, there has always been a disposition that this is the only way, that there is disaster and everything will fall apart because the cuts have been put in place. Members are not happy with some of the restored programs.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION- THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
If we talk about the herring gull program to which there has been reference today, one person out of six from that basic program was restored. He is now working out of a separate place with other support systems. Maybe that whole program is not back in the same way, but that program, the parts of it that we feel are very important for longitudinal studies, we have every right to believe can be maintained in an effective way for the purposes intended.
The notion I am trying to communicate is not so much a question on any specific, but to argue that because we did things in a particular way, because we collected tax dollars and hired certain people to do a certain job in a certain way, that is not to say there is no other way that we cannot accomplish a similar or a better end. It has been pretty impressive to see some of the communications and to witness some of the discussions that are now under way to try to address some of the problems we all accept are there. I am speaking not only of programs that have been cut but of programs that we have not yet considered, and perhaps of chemicals that may yet be discovered to be dangerous. This whole area of organizing, funding and supporting that type of activity is something that does need, not just another person here or there, but rather a constructive approach. It needs a unified, organized approach, although there are other ways. I have no doubt about this, in
which we could probably be more successful. I want to point out to Members opposite that not only have we not neglected this area, but I think in the end we will be in a better position than we have been historically.
There is another area, almost another level, that I think Members who want to address the environment have to be able to work with. There have been some comments back and forth about our need to engage the United States in a meaningful agreement in order to solve our own problems. I do not think there is any debate on that point. The approach we had been taking over the past several years in attempting to accomplish that has been very impressive. Time after time the comments made by the Hon. Member for Davenport only antagonized, polarized positions and resulted in making it more difficult to achieve that very important goal. Not only were we not doing our own homework or cleaning up our own backyard, but we were polarizing the international situation in a way that made it very difficult to reach a successful conclusion.
We have entered a new era of co-operation. I think we have a new capacity to achieve a very important and successful agreement on issues ranging from acid rain to toxic chemicals in the Great Lakes and to things which affect the environment in total, even in terms of wildlife and migratory birds and the agreements which are necessary. In the past three or four weeks we have done a number of positive and constructive things. With that as a background, we can expect to see the Minister of the Environment and the Department of the Environment fulfilling the mandate all Canadians expect and want them to fulfil. I am sure they will serve the interests of Canadians.
I am not sure how much time I have remaining, but I should like to make a final point. An idea which has been advanced in the past six or seven months concerns budget cuts, deficits and our international relationships. It started out last May and June with an OECD economic summit in Paris dealing with the environment. I attended that meeting with the then Minister of the Environment. We had a long series of discussions. The funny part is that he now seems not to recall the important discussions which occurred at that time. They indicated that we would have to consider very seriously the environment in relation to the economy, not just the cost of clean-up but the whole range of economic activity in which any modern nation is involved and the impact it will have on the economy. In fact, the conclusion reached-and I think it will be proven in the future-is that clean air is cheaper. If we do it right, most efficiently, most effectively and probably most economically, in the end we will all benefit in a large number of ways. It is not like the hard-nosed economic sense which most people would associate with things like productivity and efficiency; it is in the whole range or gambit of things which affect our daily lives, which very much affect our quality of life and the environment of the whole globe.
I should like to leave Hon. Members opposite and the House with the assurance that I for one-I may have some advantage
March 5, 1985

over Hon. Members opposite in being a little closer to it-have no question that the Government at the end of its mandate will have proven that in fact it is capable of doing what Canadians want done in the environment in a whole range of areas, from acid rain to auto emissions. We will be judged at that time. I hope Hon. members opposite in judging us will give us credit, if it is earned, when the time comes.

subsubtopic: PREMIER'S TRIAL-PRIME MINISTER'S KNOWLEDGE OF MARIJUANA FIND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I asked the Solicitor General (Mr. MacKay) to tell the House of Commons when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) was first made aware that marijuana was found in Premier Hatfield's luggage. I have asked the same question on numerous occasions, but the Government has consistently refused to answer. Why? What is it hiding? Is the Prime Minister afraid to admit that he was improperly involved in the case? This stonewall of silence would make Richard Nixon look life a rank amateur.
Yesterday the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) rose to babble on, as he usually does, when I asked my question again, notwithstanding that my question was directed to the Solicitor-General. It was interesting to see the Minister of Justice come to the defence of the Solicitor-General when, only two weeks ago, he stabbed the Solicitor-General in the back by calling for his resignation, and calling him politically incompetent.
Yesterday the Minister of Justice said that the Prime Minister was told that marijuana was found the day before charges were laid, that is, October 25. That is absolute and utter nonsense. How then can it be said that the Prime Minister did not know until October 25?
To suggest that the Prime Minister did not see a newspaper or hear a newscast between October 20 and October 25 is ludicrous and misleading. It is a deliberate misstatement of fact. Surely the Prime Minister became-

subtopic: TIRBUTE TO WORK OF WOMEN'S ORGANIZATIONS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
TIRBUTE TO WORK OF WOMEN'S ORGANIZATIONS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in British Columbia we have seen a 25 per cent reduction in public sector jobs, cuts in legal aid and rent subsidies, a freeze in welfare payments, and the withdrawal of funding for women's programs. The Socred practice of restraint has been particularly disastrous for women who have lost both the services and the jobs which existed to deliver those services.
Women are the primary beneficiaries of social services, legal aid, subsidized housing, minimum labour standards, and of a number of other programs denounced as excessive and unnecessary by the executors of restraint. In spite of all this, there exists the ongoing efforts of women in British Columbia to meet the ever-increasing economic, social, and supportive needs in their communities. I speak for my own riding of Kamloops-Shuswap which reflects much of this aftermath of restraint.
I would like to go on record in praise and support of the Kamloops Women's Resource Centre, the Kamloops & Salmon Arm Women's Emergency Shelter, the B.C. Native Women's Society, the Rape Crisis Centres, and all other services in my constituency that continue to address the burdens of women, burdens augmented as a result of economic restraint.
Women should not be expected to carry the major responsibilities for correcting inequities. It is clear that equality for all of us, in every sense of the word, requires major changes in
March 5, 1985

our economy. This can only happen when all sectors of our society share the responsibility. The Government of Canada can play its rightful role in this regard by funding those groups and organizations serving the needs of women and which support the basic principle of equality for women.

maintopic: EFFECT OF WORLD PRICES ON SUGAR PRODUCERS
EFFECT OF WORLD PRICES ON SUGAR PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to inform Parliament about the current world sugar situation and how 1,500 Canadian sugar beet producers in Quebec, Manitoba, and Alberta are being affected.
The world cost of producing cane and beet sugar is about 15 cents per pound. Eight-five per cent of world sugar trades at guaranteed domestic prices which range from 22 cents in the U.S.A. to over 40 cents a pound in Cuba. The EEC subsidy alone is 15 cents a pound. This price is guaranteed by quotas, tariffs, and subsidies. In Canada we face a situation where some 15 per cent of the world surplus determines our price, which is 4 cents per pound U.S. and, as such, we will surely lose our producers.
Canadians consume about 1 million tonnes of sugar, of which 90 per cent is imported. The amount of money leaving Canada for that sugar this year is about $80 million U.S. However, in 1980 when the price of sugar was 43 cents per pound, the cost was $800 million. Therefore, a healthy domestic sugar industry is good for consumers as protection against unstable world prices, for our foreign exchange account, for our manufacturers of machinery, and for our producers.
I strongly urge the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) and the Cabinet to make a short-term investment in this industry to ensure its survival, followed by the development of a longterm national sugar policy to put us in step with the rest of the world.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGRICULTURAL RESEARCH STATION IN TEMISCAMINGUE
ESTABLISHMENT OF AGRICULTURAL RESEARCH STATION IN TEMISCAMINGUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the determination, dynamism and undeterred confidence of socioeconomic groups in my riding will soon witness the fruitful outcome of their efforts.
A major agricultural research station is now under consideration in my riding. The probable establishment of such a station in Temiscamingue will meet an urgent need of the agricultural community and it has the unanimous support of all social and political interest groups. This is an important issue for the economy of my riding, since the proposed agricultural research station is estimated at close to $8 million and would create hundreds of jobs.
The first step towards this worthwile endeavour has been made possible through the co-operation of Agriculture Canada which will soon hire two scientists who will take up residence at and be affiliated with the University of Quebec at Rouyn with a view to making surveys and launching the agricultural research station project.
Mr. Speaker, I take this opportunity to commend Agriculture Canada for its support and co-operation in this project.
Mr. Speaker, the project will have significant economic fallouts throughout the Abitibi-Temiscamingue region and make my riding one of Canada's leading agricultural development centres. At long last will Temiscamingue see the concrete outcome of its agricultural calling.

March 5, 1985

Mr. Speaker, this week is the International Women's Week and I noticed in the annual report of the Department of Employment and Immigration that Canada Employment Centres last year allotted 32 per cent of all jobs in Canada to women. Only 32 per cent of the jobs went to women, although women account for 42 per cent of the labour force in Canada. Why the discrepancy? Even Mr. Edwards, the Assistant Deputy Minister of Employment and Immigration stated on December 5 before the Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration, and I quote:
To the extent that our job creation programs have a smaller proportion of women than their share in the labour force, that will have a depressing influence.
Even the Assistant Deputy Minister is frustrated, Mr. Speaker.
Before Christmas, we also had Mr. Justice Abella's report, which was replete with recommendations to change or correct that discrimination against Canadian women. Mr. Speaker, some in the farm community have expressed concern over the contents of the discussion paper Tax Issues in Agriculture. The paper starts with a description of the economic environment in which tax policy must be considered, and then discusses, in turn, the three issues of tax deductions of losses by part-time farmers, taxation of capital gains, and the concept of agribonds.
It is unfortunate that many of the statistics which are quoted in the paper date back to the 1981 agricultural census and 1982 Revenue Canada figures. The conclusions which could be drawn from these data would clearly be erroneous in light of the urgent situation facing agriculture.
Fortunately, tonight marks the first meeting of the parliamentary committee which will study these important agricultural tax matters. Thus, while the discussion paper has provided a useful background for consideration of these issues, it is important that the input of the agricultural community be secured through the committee's hearings.
The evidence presented to the agricultural tax committee will provide more up-to-date information on the present status
of the agriculture industry. The mandate of the agricultural tax committee is to listen to the briefs presented, and to report expeditiously to the House. It is hoped that the recommendations concerning Section 31, capital gains and agribonds, will constitute an important and vital contribution to the budgetary formation process.

Since this is International Women's Week, and with all due respect for the Chair, I feel I must inject a bit of humour into the proceedings. Ten years ago, we had International Women's Year and a year later, March 8 was designated as International Women's Day. From 1976 to 1978, the only Member of this House to mention the fact was Mr. Stanley Knowles. I wish to congratulate him on his openmindedness. He was ahead of his time.
In 1979, the House sat only two months, from October to December, as veteran Members will recall. In 1980, the House started its session in April, so of course no one had a chance to make any special reference to International Women's Day. In 1982, we had the bells episode, which we are not likely to forget, and in 1983-84 everything was back to normal. There was a reference to the good work done by our Government. In fact, this day has always been used to congratulate the Government on its good work and its effort to improve the status of women.
Today, I would like to make an exception, Mr. Speaker. 1 wish to congratulate the women of Canada. In ten years, the number of women in the House has tripled, from nine Members in 1975 to our present number of 25. This augurs well for the next generation of women Members. We have also proven that competence is not a matter of age, since we cover two generations here in the House. I therefore wish to extend my congratulations and words of encouragement to the women in this House and to the women of Canada. Keep up the good work-we are on the right track!

Mr. Speaker, if a nuclear bomb were dropped on Ottawa probably 50,000 humans would die, and every newspaper and every government in the world would call it a disaster. Yet, every year in Canada, some 50,000 human babies are murdered and it is barely news-
March 5, 1985

worthy. Perhaps it is because we do not really realize what happens when a baby is aborted.
Modern technology has enabled Dr. Bernard Nathanson to use a sonogram videotape to picture a 12-week old child in the womb being aborted. A hollow plastic tube with a sharp tip is inserted and, using suction from a vacuum, the feotus starts to be torn apart. The baby retreats helplessly to the far side to escape the device, but it pulls off her legs and disembowels her. She struggles, her head falls back, and her mouth opens in agony. Then a pair of forceps crushes the brain, and another child is murdered.
The sonogram proves beyond a shadow of a doubt that the feotus is alive. It is a human being. He or she cringes and tries to escape death. We can watch and see the gruesome picture of a child being brutally murdered. The mouth opens in a cry for help. Can't you hear that silent scream?
Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: LETTER TO MINISTER FROM NATIONAL CONGRESS OF ITALIAN CANADIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. In December, when the Minister of Finance offended the Italian
Oral Questions
Canadian community with an insensitive remark, the Prime Minister refused to apologize. He has received a copy of a letter written to the Solicitor General from the National Congress of Italian Canadians, as have I, in which they complain of the "insensitive and on its face, discriminatory comment" about the Member of Parliament for York South-Wes-ton. They used the term "Nunziata" in the letter. In the circumstances, would the Prime Minister make an apology on behalf of his Government to the Italian community, particularly to the National Congress of Italian Canadians?

subsubtopic: LETTER TO MINISTER FROM NATIONAL CONGRESS OF ITALIAN CANADIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am unaware of the specific point to which my right hon. friend refers. I would be happy to look at it.
I did receive a copy of a letter from another Liberal backbencher prior to Christmas, and I believe a copy was sent to my hon. friend. I responded in my personal name, because it reflected my views and that of my Government, and I said that as far as I was concerned, the tremendous courage, dignity, and the remarkable contribution that the Italian community has made to Canada is one that we salute. We have nothing but genuine respect and support for the magnificence of the contribution that Italian Canadians have made to Canada.
Should anything at any time be said by anyone on this side, inadvertently or otherwise, that is in any way contrary to that, of course it would be something that I would immediately regret and repudiate.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we welcome that statement, but in view of the fact that the National Congress has made what essentially amounts to a formal protest, I would like the Prime Minister to look into it formally and decide whether, in his good judgment, and reflecting the remarks he just made, a formal apology should be made.

Mr. Speaker, I would be happy to look into this. As I recall, just prior to Christmas I wrote to the Hon. Member-I believe I sent a copy to the Leader of the Opposition-and I referred to the tremendous regard in which we hold the contributions of Italian Canadians. However, I will look into this, and should there be even the slightest iota of a comment by anyone at variance with that, I assure my hon. friend that it is not the view of anyone on this side, and I am sure it wouldn't be his.

subsubtopic: NORTHERN FISHERIES DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. He knows that almost two years ago the Government of Canada and the Government of Newfoundland signed an agreement to set up a Northern Fisheries Development Corporation for fishermen north of 50. That has not yet been put in place. What has the Minister done in this respect, and can he give an assurance that the $15 million which was set aside previously for funding that corporation, or adequate funds in any event, are still in place for it?

speakeroldname: Hon. John A. Fraser (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
subsubtopic: NORTHERN FISHERIES DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his question. I must say to the Hon. Member that I am sympathetic to the concept.

Can he give that assurance, and can he tell the fishermen on the northern peninsula of Newfoundland and on the Labrador coast that he will consult with them this spring before anything specific is done?

subsubtopic: DISMISSAL OF LESBIAN PERSONNEL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Defence. Last year five qualified women in the Canadian Armed Forces, who happened to be lesbians, lost their jobs at CFS, Shelburne, in Nova Scotia, solely on the basis of their sexual orientation. In view of the fact that these women pose no threat whatsoever to Canada's national security, would the Minister explain why the women were fired, and why he continues to allow a policy on the books which discriminates so blatantly against Canadian gays and lesbians?

speakeroldname: Hon. Erik Nielsen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: DISMISSAL OF LESBIAN PERSONNEL
speechtext:

Member, having regard to his background and profession, would be the first to agree that I, being involved in that grievance process, should not be making any comment one way or the other until we establish whether or not they intend to grieve.
March 5, 1985
