What I have to add in response to the Hon. Member's question is that there are a number of sensitive areas. I am not personally sure from hearing most of the witnesses, if not all of them, of the relative factors of some of the areas for which the Canadian Wildlife Service is responsible. If we were saying that they were not to be supported, that those programs were not to be addressed in some way, I think he would have a legitimate point. On the other hand, the $1 million fund, the consultations which have been taking place with the province, with the federations involved-only one so far and one upcoming-and with others, universities included, lead me to believe that the Department, the Minister and I would be very unhappy if we were not successful in seeing all the things done on behalf of wildlife research in Canada which the Hon. Member, other Hon. Members and I would like to see done.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have proposed this motion and requested a debate and a recorded vote because there is a growing concern among Canadians that the Government lacks a real commitment to our environment.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
The Minister spoke this morning. I am sorry she is not present in the House at this time; her Parliamentary Secretary was here a minute or two ago. I deplore the practice of a Minister responsible for the subject matter of an Opposition day not being in the House to listen to the speeches, remarks, questions and complaints of the Opposition. The same practice is developing during the course of debate on pieces of legislation, where the Minister might appear in the early stages of second reading and then disappear. I hope this large majority in the House of Commons will not promote the type of indifference to Parliament which we have seen displayed on recent Opposition days. 1 wish the Minister were here. At the moment there are very few Conservative members present.
1 am not sure that we have seen in the last few months since the Government took office is a case of the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Blais-Grenier) losing battles in Cabinet over the cuts of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) or whether the Minister even participates in those battles. She has given no major address in the country on the subject of the environment. We do not know, aside from the cuts, what the Minister's plans are. We hardly know what her views are. Members of the government back-bench have said, and I paraphrase them: "Don't fight the cut-backs; wait until you see the Budget of the Minister of Finance, there are going to be even more". The Minister did not mention that in her remarks this morning. I hope she will take the earliest opportunity to do so.
I urge the Minister to explain the logic of imposing even more cuts in this vital area and to make a commitment to standing up for our environmental programs. Even on the basis of public relations, which seems to be a consideration that rules Cabinet decision-making within this Government, where the pollster has replaced the Minister in the councils of government and ranks higher in the affections of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), if the Minister thinks she got heat over the November cuts to vital areas of the Department of the
Supply
Environment, even more cut-backs will raise temperatures through the roof.
As a Canadian and as one who has had the privilege and opportunity of travelling across the land over the years, particularly by canoe with my family on many of our waterways, from one coast to the other, particularly north of the sixtieth parallel and across the Arctic Circle and into the Arctic and Pacific Oceans, I am absolutely dismayed and disgusted with the cuts to the environment made by the Government. We in British Columbia and in western Canada are absolutely outraged.
I will cite a few examples. First there is the closing or the attempt to privatize wildlife interpretation centres across Canada. There have been cut-backs in services at Webb, Saskatchewan; Creston Valley, British Columbia; Perce, Quebec; Cap Tourmente, Quebec; and Wye Marsh, Ontario. I could refer to the migratory bird sanctuary in Vancouver, the delaying of work on the Fraser River dyking project in British Columbia on the largest flyway on the west coast of North America, and the cutting of projects which monitor effects of forestry pesticides on birds in Manitoba. I could refer to the herring gull egg monitoring program. It is a $250,000 program. In relative terms that is not much money. It employed six people. It was tracing the toxic chemical impact through examination of gull eggs and analysis thereof. It is important to our understanding of the impact of these chemicals on birds or on other animals, and eventually on us. It is critical that we know precisely what is the impact in order that we can find a solution that precisely meets the danger.
What has been the Government's response? It cancelled the whole program in November. No reasons were given. After a huge public outcry, it now claims to have reinstated it. I was in Toronto yesterday and made further inquiries. Before, that project had six people and now there is only one. That person has been told just to collect the eggs, note the chemical presence and not look at the impact. What good is that?
It has cut programs to reintroduce certain fox species to Alberta and Saskatchewan where they have disappeared. It has cut the program to monitor the build-up of agricultural chemicals on birds in Alberta, particularly edible fowl. It has closed weather stations right across the country. The one in Bissett, Manitoba immediately comes to mind.
I should also like to mention the Guelph Toxicology Centre. It was to be the first of its kind. It was to monitor and assess the impact of new chemicals, but the Government cut it completely. We know that there are some 800 different chemicals in Lake Ontario alone. The Niagara River Toxics Committee found 261 chemicals in the Niagara River, 57 of which are at levels known to pose a risk to human health. Without programs like the herring gull project and the Guelph centre, how will we know what these chemicals are doing to fish in our lakes, to birds that eat the fish or to humans who drink the water or eat the fish?

The National Research Council Environmental Secretariat has been eliminated, 400 top scientists. They explained environmental issues to the country by way of lectures and publications, research on lead, PCBs, asbestos, phosphates, heavy metals, mercury and other pollutants. Where will this information come from now?
The area of the Public Service which has been savaged most severely and which really outrages me is the Canadian Wildlife Service. There were 84 people cut, 25 per cent of the entire staff. These were highly trained biologists, technicians and environmentalists. They are closing our centres across the country. The finest brains in the world, some of them, in our environment and in biology, where are they going now? They are going to the United States, Asia and Africa. They were snapped up by any country that had any interest in the environment. For three generations the Service had contributed to the best environmental service on the globe, and it has been savaged.
The Minister says that the cut-backs will not, and I use her words, adversely affect the survival of this program. What a naive attitude! It is physically impossible to cut one-quarter of the staff and have no repercussions.

And it is the same story with respect to national parks. What are the Conservatives doing this year to celebrate the one hundredth anniversary of Parks Canada? They raise entrance fees, reduce the number of employees, and force the management of many parks and reserves to eliminate some services. Nineteen hundred and eighty-five promises to be the year to visit our national parks, on one condition however: being able to get into them.
Mr. Speaker, we are incensed at the way the Government has been treating the Canadian Wildlife Service and the National Research Council. We feel insulted! Most Canadians do enjoy one common advantage: availability of and ready access to wide open spaces. Not satisfied with such savage cut-backs in our own national environment programs, the Government has also seen fit to reduce its participation in the United Nations environment program whose purpose is to seek ways to check desertic encroachment in countries such as Ethiopia where the tragic loss of agricultural land has led to untold suffering and innumerable deaths.
Aid programs of that kind are needed if we are to put an end to the dependency cycle and help other countries set up lasting agricultural programs. By reducing our participation in those programs, we can only become less familiar with the problems and contribute to make the dependency cycle even more acute.

My colleague from Davenport (Mr. Caccia), our critic on the environment, spoke eloquently this morning about acid rain killing our lakes, rivers and vegetation at an alarming
rate. The Minister of the Environment says this is no longer a priority. Her leader, the Prime Minister, seems to think that the United States Government has a case in taking no action because he says our record is not as good as theirs. The Prime Ministers says we have to do more, but the actions of his Government indicate that he is doing the reverse.
The Prime Minister says that acid rain is at the top of his list at the Summit with President Reagan in Quebec City on March 17. I congratulate him for that and wish him well, but as I have suggested in the House of Commons, he has already given the President an easy way out. The President is going to say: "Well, Brian, sure I agree, but you yourself said Canada has not done well on this, so why should we take any action if you are not?" He has already thrown his cards away.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
As our environmental critic, the Hon. Member for Davenport, was quick to point out to the Prime Minister immediately when he heard the comment, the truth is that Canada has done very well in reducing acid rain. The former Minister of the Environment in the Province of Ontario agrees. We have a program to reduce sulphur dioxide emissions by 25 per cent by 1990 and by 50 per cent by 1994. The United States does not have that program. Considering that the United States produces 19.6 million tonnes of nitric oxide per year compared with our total of only 1.7 tonnes, we know where the responsibility must be shed across our neighbourhood and across the air.
The Canadian Press now reports that the Prime Minister is anxious to telephone President Reagan in the hopes that he can get, as one official calls it, at least a token gesture on acid rain from the President. Otherwise the meeting of March 17 will be a public relations defeat for this Government. All I can tell the Prime Minister is: Beware the Ides of March, because we have been getting a busy signal from the White House on that issue ever since President Reagan took office four years ago.
The Government of Canada and the Government of Newfoundland have jointly agreed, despite the Atlantic Accord, to keep under wraps the publication of the Mobil Oil Environmental Assessment Impact Study on the production of Hibernia oil. That report was to be released two months ago. The Hibernia development will take place in the middle of one of the richest fishing grounds on the face of the globe. We urge that report to be published and to be released because it is very important environmentally.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext: Hear hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
I can turn now to the west coast. There was the tragedy of several fishermen drowning last October on the west coast when six vessels went down. There was an inquiry under Professor LeBlond which showed serious deficiencies in our forecasting. The Minister has taken some action. She has expanded the drifting buoys and she has automated shipboard programs. However, the United Fishermen and Allied Workers' Union has called for a reinstatement
March 5, 1985

of a weather ship off the west coast as absolutely necessary. The LeBlond report calls for forecasting services to fishermen to be brought up to the standards provided for aviation. I urge the Minister on behalf of British Columbia to speed up the one position for a marine forecaster instead of waiting until October, 1985 to staff that position.
The problems of the environment are not solved overnight, we know that. It requires a long-term, serious and deep commitment by the Government to be a leader in this area. Apparently the Government of Canada under this new administration wants to let others take over. The Minister suggests it is the duty of the provinces-let the provinces do it; let the private sector intervene. The Minister says that provincial Governments will pick up the slack when federal programs are cancelled. All I can say is that this is not likely, especially when you consider that in Ontario, for example, the Ontario Government has cut some $29 million out of environment programs over the past two or three years. Mr. Grossman, the Treasurer, is promising to cut every Ministry even more.
I can tell the Minister that she will not get the money from the provinces. She should realize that once she cuts a program, it is finished. I can also tell the Minister that because of the costs involved, the private sector needs some leadership, cooperation and incentives.
We take this issue immensely seriously. Every Canadian has a personal stake in protecting our environment. It is the air we breathe, the water we drink, the priceless and precious wildlife in our vast open spaces, the lakes, forests and rivers which we enjoy. Those great national treasures are fundamental to life in this country.
I do not know of anything more important to Canadians than the natural heritage with which we have been blessed. No other country comes close to the variety of geography, panorama, wildlife or space. We have one-third of the fresh water of the world. We have rivers and lakes that provide limitless recreational and camping opportunities. We have a climate and an environment which challenges us in each of the four seasons.
Our national character has certainly been shaped by our geography. Our national character has been fashioned by the type of country we have been given and with which we have been blessed. For a Government not to recognize that, but to diminish and denigrate the priority of preserving that heritage, is beyond my understanding. I cannot tolerate it. Everywhere I go, and this is shared by my colleagues, at every public platform, at every question and answer session that we have in our universities, high schools and in our groups, the Canadian people raise this subject.
Two weeks ago I had a town hall meeting in Vancouver Quadra which 900 people attended. The environmental questions were absolutely uppermost on the minds of the people. Why is it, blessed as we have been, that the Government, as the custodian of our heritage and our natural environment, allows the cuts to be so shamelessly taken? Who sets these priorities? Why does the Minister not stand up for them? If she has not succeeded against the Minister of Finance (Mr. Supply
Wilson) or the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret), why does she not at least have the guts to say so? She should take that responsibility off her shoulders and say, "No.
I cannot succeed, but I will not be blamed by the people of Canada for what we are doing to our environment".

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
I believe that is why Canadians have reacted so strongly to the Government's tampering with the protection of the environment. That is why, since those cuts were known after the November 8 statement of the Minister of Finance, our Party has led the fight in the House to reverse some of those cuts. It is also why we in this Party will continue to lead that fight if the Government persists on this very dangerous and self-defeating course. We will do it in Parliament. We will do it in the country. We will fix the record in the public's mind, because what is being left undone by this Government is something that can never be repaired.
The environment is a permanent heritage. The renewable resources of Canada depend on it. The well-being and health of our citizens depend on it. The life that we have been given and the welcoming of tourists from all over the world depend on it. It is part of the Canadian heritage and character. It goes right to the fibre and bone of Canadian intuition and instinct. If the Government does not understand that, it does not understand the country. If the Minister wants to regain some of the promise she has lost, she had better stand up to her colleagues soon. She should go to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and say, "Look, I am being pilloried from one end of the country to the other and I am not being allowed to do my duty, to fulfil my mandate or to fulfil the expectations which the Canadian people have in me and in this Government. Either allow me to do it, Mr. Prime Minister, or relieve me of the responsibility".

Mr. Speaker, I enjoyed the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) and I certainly agree with much that he said. Of course, to many of us who have been concerned about the environment and the erosion of the environment over the last few decades it is refreshing to hear the Leader of the Liberal Party expressing those sentiments. I wish those sentiments had been expressed many years ago. I am afraid that the record of his Party when in government in dealing with Eldorado Nuclear and the waste and spoilage which that corporation caused in many parts of the country is not favourable. One could mention the testing of herbicides and pesticides and the pollution of ground water on the Prairies that the Department of Agriculture of previous Liberal Governments allowed. One could go on to mention waste disposal in Canada.
My question is: Is this a conversion of the Liberal Party? If the Liberal Party ever regains power, will we see a new agenda for the environment of Canada? Will he give us the commitment that the errors of the past are indeed of the past and that a new Liberal Government will set a new agenda for the environment of Canada?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there need not be any new commitment. The commitment has been there throughout the years of Liberal administrations.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Saint-Maurice (Mr. Chretien), had the honour to inaugurate and establish more national parks than any other Minister in the history of the country. We have been at the leading edge of environmental protection. The Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), when he was Minister of the Environment, brought the acid rain question to the attention of Canadian people, as did his predecessor, Mr. Roberts. Our record stands on its own. We have no apologies to make. I have no doubt that the Canadian people, in their minds, will recognize that, whatever reasons they may have had for changing the administration on September 4, our commitment to the environment was not among those reasons.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) a question. First, I would like to note that I was not smiling at his comments with respect to the intervention of the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark), but merely at his extraordinary
gesticulations and comments about what happened within the Conservative Cabinet. I am not there, so I am sure I do not know. I am not sure whether the habit of the former Government was such that he knew that his Minister of the Environment was really impotent in the face of Liberal Cabinet Ministers.
My question is: Is he proud of the Liberal record as it relates to the environment?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I could not be more proud of the record of Liberal Governments over the years as being the leaders and the pioneers of environmental protection. Certainly I am proud of that record.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner). I think be might want to take the opportunity to distribute the credit for public awareness of the acid rain problem more widely than he did a minute ago when he gave all the credit to the former Minister of the Environment, the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), and the former Member from Toronto, Mr. Roberts. Is the Leader of the Opposition not aware that a special subcommittee of the House was set up to study acid rain, that it travelled the country and the world, produced reports and played a great part in creating the public awareness which we now have, of which we should be taking advantage? Out of respect for Parliament and the work of that committee, I think that the Leader of the Opposition should have something more to say.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for bringing that to my attention. With only 20 minutes in which to speak, I cannot cover all of the good aspects of what Parliament has accomplished. I second him in lauding the work of that committee which, after all, was set up by the previous Liberal Government under the Ministry of John Roberts. Our former colleague, Ron Irwin, then the Member for Sault Ste Marie, was the Chairman of that committee and did an excellent job. I would not have had time to mention that had the hon. gentleman not been kind enough to bring it to our attention.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) mentioned the Toxicology Centre at the University of Guelph which was cut out by the Government. I think that was a tremendous blow to the whole policy on toxicology. It was a model idea because it drew together federal and provincial Governments, the private sector, the University of Toronto and the University of Guelph. It was to be a centre of excellence which would not only develop new techniques, designs and models for handling toxicology issues, but it was also to be a national centre for the entire country which would train young scientists. It is a tragedy that that centre was cut out. Over a period of several years it would have received $16 million from the federal Government, $16 million from the provincial Government and about $8 million from the private sector. It really grew together in one location, under the sponsorship and co-operation of two large national
March 5, 1985

universities. The most frustrating and maddening part of this whole episode was not only that it was cut out after a director had been appointed, with the resultant floundering, but that I received no real answer from the Minister when I asked her in the House why it was being cut out.
Everyone seems to be concerned about pesticides and toxins in our environment which affect our health. We have concern with cancer and so on. The chairman of the board was a cancer specialist at the University of Toronto. When I asked a question of the Minister, she made some comment that the cost had jumped up from-I have forgotten the figure-about $15 million to $50 million. But in fact the actual cost of the plant was going to be about $21 million. Obviously, the Minister cannot know about each decision, but one would think that when a major national institution of this type is being wiped out by the Government, the Minister would take the time to familiarize herself with the situation.
There was an adjournment debate on this subject. The Parliamentary Secretary or the Minister usually reads from a prepared script with all the facts, figures and details in it. It was very disconcerting that the Minister made a couple of comments about the centre but did not go into the details. Obviously she still did not know what the centre was about or the national role it was designed to play.
So as a comment I will say that I was pleased that the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition mentioned this centre. I think it is one of the most terrible decisions made by this Government since it was appointed. I would like to ask the Leader of the Opposition if he agrees with me.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-THE ENVIRONMENT

I could not have put it better, Mr. Speaker. I know of the Hon. Member's abiding concern for the environment, coming from the place of location of the Algoma Central Railway. I have travelled on that train up to Wawa with the Hon. Member and others and I know what a great part of the country he lives in.
These cut-backs are not only a blow to the research which needs to be done but they are a tremendous blow to the scientific community of this country. Something we have tried to build up over the course of many years is our expertise. Dismissing this project, sabotaging the Canadian Wildlife Service, will just lead to the export of the expertise which we have developed over three generations.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would have hoped, in speaking in this debate on the environment today, that it would be treated in more of a non-partisan way. One would have hoped that Hon. Members, by the time they managed to get elected by their communities across this country, would have read enough, or know enough generally, to understand what is happening in the world. Right now, today, about six species of life on this planet are becoming extinct. What is happening around the world, Mr. Speaker, are changes to the basic architecture of the living environment which are irreversible. We have the introduction of certain toxics and all kinds of different materials as the result of the development of cities, transportation, the use of jet aircraft. All kinds of developments are changing our environment forever. We are tinkering with the basic living components of the world. I would have hoped that in a country such as Canada where we have a very literate and well educated population, a country with free press and excellent media, these kinds of irresponsible and rash decisions which are being made by the new Government simply would not occur. I would also hope, Mr. Speaker, that by now, with the thousands and tens of thousands of representations which have been made by well educated, interested and concerned Canadians to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and to the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Blais-Grenier), the kinds of cuts which were made would not have happened and debates such as this simply would not have been necessary.
I do not think I can stress enough, Mr. Speaker, the real need for this Parliament to come to grips with the issue of the environment when we talk about sending the MV Arctic up into Zone I ice knowing that it is contrary to the regulations of Lloyd's of London and contrary to the Arctic Waters Pollution Prevention Act. I see the Parliamentary Secretary shaking his head, but I know in fact it is true, Mr. Speaker. 1 have looked into the matter. It is only through an Order in Council that that particular tanker is going to be allowed into the Canadian Arctic.
When we examine the cuts, Mr. Speaker, I think we have to understand something about the person who made them. A recent article written by Warren Caragata, I believe, revealed something with which the Prime Minister should have taken issue before the Minister's appointment. Since it was not taken issue with before the appointment of the present Minister of

March 5, 1985

the Environment, it should take place now. With the same reasoning and on the same grounds that the Prime Minister accepted the resignation of the former Minister of National Defence, he should request the Minister of the Environment to step down from her Crown portfolio. The article is headlined, "Called Unfit in Previous Job, Tory Minister Sues Over Firing". The former Minister of National Defence rose in this House and said that he could not actively and properly pursue his lawsuit against the Citizen newspaper here in Ottawa as a Minister of the Crown. Using the same kinds of rules and guidelines used by the Prime Minister in accepting the resignation of the Minister of National Defence, I believe he should accept or request the resignation-even if it is only temporary-of the Minister of the Environment. Because of what is filed in the court documents, it is truly unusual for the Minister to remain in her portfolio while the air is coloured by these matters. I quote from the article by Warren Caragata:
Court documents quote Mrs. Blais-Grenier as saying that she was accused of falsifying minutes of meetings, hysteria, incompetence and intellectual dishonesty, was ultimately fired, and was unable to find similar work in the area of workplace health and safety.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to make sure that the Right Hon. Member from High River is aware of the situation, I will quote from an article in The Globe and Mail. I believe it is quite proper that this kind of information be made available to the Hon. Members of this House and to the general public. It is printed in the paper. The article goes on to state:
The fashion in which she was dismissed raised doubts about her competence, she said, and made it difficult, if not impossible, to find an equivalent post in the health and safety field.
Environmental groups and one source within the Environment Department itself, meanwhile, contend that Mrs. Blais-Grenier has shown similar behavior over the cuts in the wildlife service. Most asked, however, that their names not be used.
Ken Brynaert, vice-president of the Canadian Wildlife Federation, complained that, despite requests for meetings with the Minister to discuss the cuts, the association has not yet had even a reply. "You can't negotiate with her," he said. "She has been protected by her office."
Early in her tenure, the Minister confided in a private conversation that she had decided against a full range of briefings by her officials on the workings of the department.
She refused briefings, she related, because she did not want to be confused and because she had decided to learn on the job.
When you tie that article into the mosaic of what has occurred-and I hope the Hon. Member from High River listens as I tie together the reason for introducing that information into this debate-you can see why Canadians are deeply troubled by what was said during the Conservative campaign until September 4 and what has occurred since. They had no mandate from the scientific or corporate communities, the voters or any private interest group which made themselves available to committees of this House on which to base those cuts. They were made for other reasons, and I intend to reveal some of the reasons why I believe those kinds of savage cuts were made. Canadians have time and again indicated they are prepared to take a lower standard of living and pay more taxes to preserve the heritage of this country.
In a November news release, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) made it clear what his intentions were. He intended to cut S8.7 million from environment services, which encompass federal programs in wildlife, water, environmental protection and atmospheric services. He intended to cut $5 million from the Environment Secretariat and all its research facilities. He intended to cut Parks Canada operations by $19.5 million and to get rid of the Guelph Toxicology Centre at $5.4 million, as well as take $10.5 million away from Parks and Weather Services. We can discuss at greater length this matter and the loss of lives which are perhaps related to some of those cuts. But let us look at what the Conservatives had to say during the campaign related to the environment. I quote from the PC campaign handbook on the environment:
As a government:
We will make transboundary pollution problems the government's top
environmental priority.
What happened, Mr. Speaker? They get rid of the herring gull program, something which was recognized around the world as a base line scientific project providing important information on toxicology and the impact of materials coming particularly from the Niagara River, the Love Canal, S Site, Hyde Park and other dumps on the American side, as well as what is happening to Great Lakes water quality. The Parliamentary Secretary knows full well the pressures coming from Cabinet not to allow committees of this House to hear certain witnesses on matters related to problems with the Great Lakes water quality. That is shameless commentary on a mandate which was improperly and irregularly taken from the Canadian people to seat them on that side of the House. The handbook goes on to say:
Instead of relying exclusively on diplomatic intiatives by the Minister of the Environment, as the current government has done, a P.C. government will also engage the Prime Minister and the Minister of External Affairs in top-level efforts with their U.S. counterparts on such bilateral issues as acid rain, Niagara River pollution, and the Garrison Diversion Project.
I hope to learn during this debate from the government side what these steps have been to date and what kinds of ameliorative actions there have been in the U.S. Not one single nickel has been spent since September 4 by the Environmental Protection Agency from its superfund for the clean-up of the Love Canal, Hyde Park or any of the other dumps. As to
March 5, 1985

Garrison, we are fortunate that finally Congress has agreed to a sensible position, at least temporarily. But acid rain has yet to receive the kind of attention either in this country or in the U.S. that it deserves. We still have as much acid rain today as we had on September 4, if not more. The handbook goes on to read:
We accept and will act to implement all 38 recommendations of the all-Party House of Commons Sub-committee on Acid Rain.
Not one has been implemented since September 4, Mr. Speaker. These are great promises, but let us go on and look at the really key statement related to the cuts. It reads:
We will conduct a thorough review of all Environment Canada programs and expenditures, based on the twin principles of sunset laws and zero-based budgeting.
Where do they talk about 28 per cent cuts? It simply does not appear in the documents on which the Conservatives were elected. So let us look at what was cut.
The reduction of the Canadian Wildlife Service of Environment Canada by 84 person-years and $3.8 million will eliminate most of the Wildlife Research and Interpretation Branch, one of three CWS branches. Most of a series of projects grouped together in a program called Wildlife Research are to be cut. They involve 50 person-years and $2.2 million, and the operation of five Interpretaion Centres involving 32 person-years and $1.2 million. The Habitat Acquisition Fund, $400,000 and two person-years will also be eliminated. That includes most of the work carried out under the authority of the Canada Wildlife Act passed by this Parliament some 12 years ago. So those go out the door.
Let us look at some of the other things which will be added to the burden on the Canadian environment. First is the effects of toxic chemicals on birds protected by the Migratory Birds Convention Act. Under that, the monitoring of effects of agricultural insecticides and herbicides on the Prairies is gone. Then we have monitoring of contaminants in birds on the St. Lawrence River and its estuary in Quebec. That is gone. The monitoring of the effects of presticides and herbicides and sewage and everything else on the Fraser River estuary, that is gone. Then there is the identifying and monitoring of the occurrence and effects of toxic substances in herring gulls and other fish-eating birds on the Great Lakes. That matter has been raised many times in this House and I must say that my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) described it quite accurately as being a fraud. The Minister announced it was going to be cut and then, under pressure from the public, said it was reinstated. Many people in Canada, certainly in Ontario, expected that the program was being reinstated when the Minister put out a press release saying it was going to be reinstated. But we now know that only one person out of the six was reinstated. I have a few comments here from an article by Michael Keating which 1 think are worthy of being on the record. He said:
Last month, Mrs. Blais-Grenier announced that "the detection and monitoring of toxic substances in herring gulls will be continued," although some of the work would be done by another government laboratory.
Supply
However, the second laboratory is already fully booked with other work. There is no indication that it is equipped for-or has the time or expertise to handle- the specialized work of gull egg analysis.
In the meantime, the chemist in Hull who did the analysis of chemicals in gull eggs collected from around the Great Lakes has found a job in another department.
Only D. V. Weseloh, the biologist at the centre of the controversy, has been reinstated and he has been told only to collect the eggs, but not to make observations about the health of the gull colonies.
Mr. Weseloh and his assistant have previously found defects in gulls such as crossed bills, deformed feet, poor embryos, thin eggshells and other signs that pollution affects the birds' health.
Mr. Weseloh has been told not to bother recording these observations in the future.
What kind of responsible Government would tell a professional biologist that if he sees deformities or unusual biological occurences, he should not observe it. "Whatever you do, do not write it down. We do not want any more of that kind of stuff in the newspaper". If you look at the people whose jobs have been eliminated across Canada, Mr. Weseloh was the only wildlife veterinary pathologist in Canada. This morning the Minister said that the cuts were designed to get rid of people who were redundant and extravagant. That particular person was responsible for some of the key work related to migratory birds. He is responsible for the key work being done on the anaesthesizing of grizzly and polar bears, a very tricky and highly specialized field.
This cut will perhaps endanger not only biologists who work with bears in the parks and so on but others as well. When you find someone that highly specialized and doing some important international work, you cannot describe it as redundant or extravagant, nor can you claim it is replaceable. There is no one in any university or hospital in this country who can or will replace that kind of expertise. It is those kinds of savage and unnecessary, ill-thought out and irresponsible cuts that this House should be demanding be reinstated.
Another cut involves monitoring effects of forestry insecticides on birds in New Brunswick. A little bit of that has been replaced because of public pressure. Yet the Minister said this morning she was very proud of what she has done in the Department regarding these cuts. Those were her own words this morning. Under the program for the rehabilitation of endangered species, Mr. Speaker, studies on the reintroduction of peregrine falcons in eastern Canada have been stopped. The program for the reintroduction of the pine marten to Newfoundland, that is gone. The program for the reintroduction of the swift fox, black-footed parrot and the greater prairie chicken to the prairie provinces, that is gone. Biolectronics services are gone. Studies being done on the porcupine caribou and George River cariboo as well as on the Beverley-Kaminurial caribou herd are all gone. Also cut was the study on the impact of development on migratory birds using the Fraser River estuary. Environment impact assessment has been chopped. Support to federal services such as national parks and other federal lands, work on marten and peregrine falcons, wolves, elk, bears and caribou is all gone.

March 5, 1985
Supply
Under forestry, funds for studying the effects of spraying on migratory birds, song birds and wildlife habitat, which includes the effect that cutting and spraying practices have on small rodents, are all gone. The wildlife interpretation centres and habitat acquisition is gone.
It was not only the Minister of the Environment who was involved in these cuts, Mr. Speaker. This was a very carefully and methodically thought out process which obviously occurred at high levels within the Conservative Party. All of the networking programs which are under way at the NRC were chopped as well.
Funds were cancelled for the following programs under the air sub-committee: environmental impact of emissions from residential combustion appliances; analytical techniques for polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in environmental media; indoor air quality and human exposure to indoor air pollutants in Canada; effects of gaseous pollutant mixtures on crops and forests; scientific criteria for the atmospheric deposition of acidifying substances in Canada; and aerial transmissions of microbial aerosols and its implications for human and animal health.
A report on fetal hazards, which was requested by Health and Welfare Canada and the Canadian Medical Association, was in its second draft when it was cancelled. A study on the pulmonary effects on humans of the wood processing industry, which was requested by the woodworkers in British Columbia, is cancelled. Also cancelled is the study on the environmental effects of salmonella on human health. Mr. Speaker, a study on the effects of poisons on human health has been cancelled. Also cancelled were studies on the aerial transmissions of microbial aerosols, the effects of manganese in the Canadian environment, and the effects of environmental lead on children.
Earlier today Conservative Members were asking my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill, what is wrong with lead. The Government does not want to know. The Royal Society Commission on Lead asked for that study to be done, and then it was cancelled by the new Tory Government. This was a study of the effects of environmental lead on children in daycare centres near stop signs with cars stopping and starting all the time. Also cancelled were studies on the effects and interactions of trace elements on the cardiovascular system and on efficient monitoring of the environment for toxic elements and their compounds. Why would a government want to get rid of that kind of program?
A study on the effects of mine tailing wastes in the Canadian environment, requested by the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, was cancelled. A study on the effects of acid precipitation and toxic waste dumps on the quality of ground water in Canada was cancelled. How can we possibly accumulate the kind of research information we need on acid rain if these kinds of projects, which do not cost very much, are cancelled by the Government?
A study on pyrethroids and their effects on man and terrestrial and aquatic systems, requested by the National Research Council, was cancelled. At the time of cancellation, scientific analysis was over 90 per cent complete. An updated scientific analysis of the key issues in the assessment of polychlorinated biphenyls, which was requested by the Ontario Government, was cancelled. A study on PCBs, one of the most chronic and debilitating toxics in our environment, was cancelled. A study on the scientific analysis of the criteria for assessing the impact of organic chemicals, including pesticides, on ground water resources in Canada was requested by the NRC and then cancelled. What kind of government does not want to know what the effects of pesticides and chemicals are on ground water? Ground water provides sustenance to the majority of Canadians, but the Government does not want to know what the effects of toxic or chemical pesticides on ground water are.
A study on the scientific analysis of the criteria for assessing the impact of phenolic compounds on man and his environment was cancelled. Studies on cadmium in the aquatic environment, viruses in the water, biologically available metals in sediments, metal mixtures in the environment and viral infections of fish and their impact on fisheries in Canada were cancelled.
All one has to do is to look at the headlines in recent months to see how the public has received these cuts. The Tories delivered the crullest cuts to our wildlife. They cut 3 per cent across the board, except for the Canadian Wildlife Service where they cut 28 per cent. Mr. Speaker, this is irresponsible and reprehensible and the Minister should step down from her portfolio immediately.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the hon. gentleman who just spoke for his speech. I can assure the translator and the young lady who is taking dictation that I will not read such long words as the hon. gentleman had to do in his speech to get his point across. I congratulate the hon. gentleman on his speech.
I think that the cuts in the Department of the Environment can be divided into three categories: bad, worse, and ridiculous. I will give the House some examples. According to the Minister' own press release of November, 1984, she said that in Parks Canada improvements to existing parks, including maintenance complexes, visitor service facilities, staff accommodation, restorations, interpretation centres, and new land acquisition, will be cancelled to save $18.7 million in 1985-86. That can be classified as bad enough. It meets the Tory philosophy of cutting back immediately on what they think should not be continued.
I will now go to the next section, which I classify as being worse. It says that revenues will be increased by $9.2 million from increased entrance fees, camping fees, fishing permits, canal fees, golf course fees and utility fees. The new fee structure, according to the Minister, will more closely reflect those for similar services offered in the private sector. That is even worse, Mr. Speaker, than the first set of cuts that the Minister announced for Parks Canada. That is worse because
March 5, 1985

it affects every single person entering a national park. Those increases in the charges were made with no thought whatsoever to how it would affect all the people. According to this, anyone who lives within a national park will now have to pay $30 to go trouting. Those cuts are worse.
We now come to what I would call ridiculous and impossible cuts under Parks Canada. The first sentence indicates that alternative guide services, such as self-guided and volunteer guided tours, will be implemented on interpretation trails throughout the park system. That is absolutely ridiculous, Mr. Speaker. That is impossible. How can you have volunteer self-guided tours in national parks? As I mentioned to the Minister before, you have to erect signs saying "Enter at your risk". You would probably have to leave a telephone number for search and rescue on the same signs. Can you imagine people visiting our national parks, going among the forests and bears on a self-guided tour? That is plainly and simply ridiculous. I presume that the Minister has enough in her budget to paint those signs to say "Enter at your own risk".
I will now turn to the cuts in the atmospheric environmental service. That is a service which really cannot be cut at all. When the Conservatives were running for office, they said they were going to increase that service and provide better weather forecasting. They were going to spend more money on personnel in the weather offices in eastern Canada. This was one of the big election promises. The cuts are bad in that operations will be streamlined by integrating weather stations at five locations: Goose Bay, Sept-Iles, Port Hardy, Prince George and Fort Nelson. That is bad enough. The next section, which I would classify as being worse, reads that according to the Minister, weather observing stations at Eddy Point, Nova Scotia, and Bissett, Manitoba, as well as the North Bay, Ontario weather office, will be closed. Rather than the promises to increase personnel in the weather offices throughout the country and to improve forecasts for fishermen and farmers, weather offices have been closed. These cuts could be classified as being worse.
We come to the third category which I would classify as ridiculous and impossible. The Minister says that those people wishing weather information additional to that provided by the media will be charged a fee for this service. That is just plain insane. The Minister has tried to skirt around the question of how one can charge people for phoning the weather office. I brought this question up in the House one day with particular reference to fishermen and those whose health and safety are affected. The Minister said in the Chamber, in grandiose fashion, that fishermen will not have to pay. For a moment I reflected on the generosity of the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Blais-Grenier) in at least retracting somewhat on that policy. However, I began to question how one could know if it was a fisherman who was phoning the weather office. Will he have to give his social insurance number so that the Department of Fisheries and Oceans can verify if he is a fisherman? Even if it could be determined that a fisherman was phoning the weather office, by what means could he be charged? When
Supply
I pursued this further with the Minister, I asked her the same question. She had to admit in the Chamber what she was bound to find out anyway, that she was incorrect. Everyone will be charged, including the fishermen and those people whose health and safety could be affected by that information. There was no way to exempt fishermen.
Today there is no possible way to charge someone for phoning the weather office. One would have thought that the Minister of the Environment would have discovered that. The CRTC will not allow her to do what she had asked Bell Canada to do, which was to make the collection for the Department. That cannot be done because it violates their licence.
There is only one option that the Minister can use to collect $1.3 million from Canadians who want to know what the weather will be but missed the forecast on the TV or radio. The only way to collect that money, which is listed in the Estimates as revenue of that Department, is for the weather office personnel to call back someone phoning the office in order to charge them for the call. In other words, it is giving more work to weather forecasters than they can do in the weather office.
Let us continue with the Minister's press release. There is a section which is bad with respect to the Environmental Protection Service. The Minister announced that waste management activities will be cut to save $ 1.2 million. That is bad enough because we have wastes in this country that are dangerous to Canadians. They are scattered in provincial jurisdictions, in vacant mines and in old buildings in the middle of the countryside. According to our regulations, there must be some monitoring taking place. There are provincial jurisdictions with provincial rules which do not even permit wastes to be transported across provincial boundaries without the permission of that provincial jurisdiction. It is detrimental to cut $1.2 million from a branch that deals with the safety of Canadians.
Even worse, toxicology research will be phased down with cut-backs on specific projects in certain provinces such as in your home province, Mr. Speaker. The ridiculous category concerns wildlife interpretation and research which will be restricted to migratory birds and endangered species. It is not possible to cut even $100,000 from the Canadian Wildlife Service without affecting migratory birds and endangered species.

speechtext: We did it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
That is exactly what I wanted someone to say. The Minister also said that "we did it." She cut back on the scientific research that was being done on the shorebirds in British Columbia. They were migratory birds. She cut back on the entire research team that was studying the effects of pesticides, insecticides and herbicides on ducks, migratory birds, in the Prairies. That experiment should not have been discontinued because the research project was only half completed. Although the research team consisted of five or seven people, how important was that research? They discovered that the aerial spray that was used on those farms in western

March 5, 1985
Supply
Canada had actually caused the death of young ducklings. The question which arises is, how did it cause the death of young ducklings? Was it caused by the infecting of the food that young ducks ate, or was it actually caused directly to the duck itself? Those questions remain unanswered because that experiment on migratory birds has been cancelled. According to the Minister and the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret), who is sitting here this afternoon, who stated in his Estimates that migratory birds would not be affected, we are now aware that they are affected by those cuts.
Let us deal with endangered species. As the Member from the New Democratic Party mentioned, the experiments with the perigrine falcon are finished. In Newfoundland, at the request of the Newfoundland Government, the Department of the Environment under the previous Government embarked on a project to save the pine martin in that province. That project has been cut. Two endangered species in Atlantic Canada have been affected by these simple cuts, as the Minister says, in the Canadian Wildlife Service.
The Minister stated recently that she was implementing another man-year to continue monitoring the porcupine cariboo herd that travels from the Northwest Territories into the Yukon, down through Alaska. In other words, this involves an agreement with two Territories, the United States and Canada. However, there was a cut in the monitoring management of another cariboo herd in this country through these cuts in the Canadian Wildlife Service. That cariboo herd is in Labrador in Newfoundland. We all saw on television 10,000 cariboo going down the river. That entire initiative that was instituted by the federal Government upon the request of the Governments of Quebec and Newfoundland has been wiped out by these Estimates. The other one, apparently by reinstating one man-year according to the Minister, has been reinstated, that is the one that deals with an agreement with the United States. But the one on the Labrador coast, the Georges River herd, the largest in the country, is not being reinstated.
When the Minister and the President of the Treasury Board, who is in his seat today, make statements that they are not going to touch endangered species projects and migratory birds projects, I wish they would look at what exactly they are cutting because therein you would find the contradiction, Sir.
The debate so far has only dealt with the high profile items cut in this Department. Staying with the Canadian Wildlife Service cuts, there are grave consequences to the cutting of projects within the Wildlife Service that have to do with birds that are not endangered species and that have to do with animals that are not endangered species. I refer specifically to the function that was always there of the Canadian Wildlife Service to provide information to the Pest Control Division of the Federal Department of Agriculture for the registration of herbicides and insecticides.
The input into that very vital operation of the federal Government in the Department of Agriculture is required from the Department of National Health and Welfare. It is
also required from industry, but the only people who supplied the information on animals and birds was the Canadian Wildlife Service. They supplied it sometimes acting in conjunction with the National Research Council. How important is that, Mr. Speaker? How important is that cut made in eastern Canada to discontinue experiments being done on aerial sprays as it relates to insecticides? I will tell you how important it is, Mr. Speaker. If we go back about 20 years we will recall the registration of DDT in Canada. We all know what happened. Nobody in his right mind in this country today would say that we should approve DDT to be used as an aerial spray to get rid of the balsam woolly aphid, or the hemlock looper. No, not today. We moved from that particular product into phenitroth-ion and then when the research work was done on that, we moved into matracil, and we discovered, by looking at the research that was done on the wildlife in this country, that these particular products had problems. They, in effect, in the amounts being used in the products, were killing birds.
Why is that important? Birds are the natural predator of the very insect that we were trying to get rid of. Birds ate the spruce budworm. You would think, over a period of time, that if the budworm increased its population, birds would also increase their population. But there was a new element put into the environment, that of the aerial spraying of chemicals.
The Government of Canada has been instrumental in the world in trying to find a solution to the problem of chemical spraying. I suppose some of the Members here who have delved into the subject would know about the very valuable research being done by Dr. Schmirnoff in the Province of Quebec who invented BT, which is a non-chemical substance. Why? Because the chemicals killed the birds. In the beginning, with the types of chemicals we were using, it also killed the fish. It also gave rise to such terrible things as Rey's syndrome in children.
I see, Mr. Speaker, that you are telling me that I have a minute left. I wish I could go on until the official vote or until the Minister steps into the House so that I could tell her where she is wrong as far as these cuts are concerned.
To conclude, the Minister's cuts can be divided into bad, worse, and ridiculous. Let me add another category, that of impossible. The most important part of these cuts deals with things that cannot be cut. The government has to realize that there are certain Departments of the Government in this country today that are really operating on a shoe-string. To use those Departments for cuts is unfair and against the wishes of the Canadian people.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am glad to thank the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker) for his lucid view of the effects of the Minister's cuts on our environment. Why does he feel the Minister was wrong in this respect? He indicated her views were somewhat incorrect. Would he expand on that?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the most important aspect has really been lost to date by some of the discussions involving the Canadian Wildlife Service. The President of the Trea-
March 5, 1985

sury Board just made a comment, and I will overlook it because he was lost when he issued his financial statement. There were words in that financial statement that were not carried through in the cuts.
The reason I made the statement is that when you remove a service from such a vital area of input as the use of chemicals, not on the ground but in the air, and when you remove an input from the registration of a chemical that is being sprayed over an entire province and you remove a vital aspect in determining whether or not to use that chemical, how long you are going to use it, or what size the droplet will be, when you remove that vital information that nobody else is going to provide, then you are getting into an area that is very very dangerous.
If you look at Canadian history and examine what has happened over the years in this country, you see that there are people who have written books on the subject and articles that said that perhaps our mistake happened when we used chemicals in aerial sprays. Perhaps that is what happened. Perhaps we should be looking at what they do in Europe in controlled woodlots. Perhaps we should have bird nurseries instead of using chemicals. Perhaps there are other options that are open.
When one makes an across-the-board cut and says for public consumption, "I am not going to touch migratory birds and endangered species", the ordinary person says, "That's good. We all love endangered species. We all love migratory birds". In that way one gets away with the cut on the basis of immediate reaction from the public generally. Nobody looks at the long-term effects or the drastic effects that are in place. You are not looking at birds that were not endangered, you are looking at species that were not endangered, nor at migratory birds, and there is the whole point. Down the road, a future Government will come along and reinstate every one of those cuts. If things keep going the way they are, if the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) keeps forcing Ministers to cut the budgets of their Departments ad hoc, if he keeps doing that in conjunction with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), the Government will not last beyond the next election.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to participate in the debate on this non-confidence motion before the House. Actually I am surprised that the Opposition has decided to condemn the Government for its negligent and irresponsible approach to protection and management of the environment. It would be shocking if that were true, if it had some basis in fact, but the resolution itself has no basis in fact. I should like to try to point that out during the next few minutes.
When we look at the environment and its protection, we have to look at more than just what is within the jurisdiction of one Minister or that Minister's Department. For example, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Government made a substantial and important move in appointing the Cabinet of the new Government and in appointing the Minister of State
Supply
for Forestry (Mr. Merrithew). The Minister of State for Forestry is perhaps as important to environmental issues as any other person aside from the Minister herself. For that reason, we see right off the bat that environmental issues have at least two strong supporters with Ministries in Cabinet at the present time. That is a pronounced and dramatic improvement in the situation. In fact, it is the first time in almost two decades that an independent portfolio has been created in the Government of Canada to take care of forestry. What could be more important to environmental matters than taking care of our forests and the natural habitat of much of Canada's wildlife?
The Opposition has gone on at some length in regard to the substantial cuts made to environmental programs. Yes, there have been changes in priorities and cuts have been made. However, let us take a look at the budgetary summaries. I think they speak for themselves. In the Minister's summary it was suggested that almost $727 million will be spent by the Department of Environment in 1985-86. If we compare that figure with the one for last year, there is a $15 million cut, but we have to determine how much $15 million is in relation to the $727 million. We will soon see that the decrease is a little over 2 per cent. That hardly reflects the kinds of accusations which opposition caucuses have been making in this debate today. If we take into account the toxicology support which the Government is providing at the present time, I am told that we will find that the budget for environmental matters is actually up 3.8 per cent.
I could be a little more specific in terms of some of the support which is being provided to groups and organizations and to various issues across the country, but it is important to realize that there are more issues in the environment than the ones noted so far by the Opposition. There is continued support at the same levels to groups such as the Canadian Association of Geographers, the International Geograhic Union, and the Canadian Council of Resource and Environment Ministers. There is continued support at the same levels as those of the past for the Canadian Wildlife Federation and the Canadian Nature Federation. There is an increase in the budget for the Creston Valley Wildlife Management Authority. There is a new figure for the Wildlife Habitat Canada Foundation, a new injection of $1.3 million, which the Opposition did not point out during the debate so far. There is another increase to the Fur Institute of Canada of $500,000. If we continue through the Estimates we find an increase to the James Bay Agreement project, to the Red River Ring Dyking project and to the Qu'Appelle Valley project in Saskatchewan.
Perhaps we could look at the reductions. I suggest these have been omitted by the Opposition as well. If we look at the specifics-and perhaps I will not go into them-we will quickly see that the reductions probably reflect those programs introduced by the former Government in its last ditch attempts to be re-elected.
There are other contributions which I think are significant in terms of the over-all objectives of the Government. For instance, there is the contribution to the National and Provin-

cial Parks Association of Canada. It has been increased by 50 per cent this year. There is a new contribution to the Interagency Forest Fire Centre, which is important if wildlife is to be preserved and enhanced. We must ensure that our forest fire service is as good as can be. I would be pleased to enter into debate on the subject of specific cuts. I would be the first to say that I would rather not see cuts made to any organization, for certainly they-and this one in particular-play an important role in protecting environmental matters in Canada, wildlife in particular. During the discussion with the Executive Vice-President of that group, Mr. Brynaert, I had the opportunity to ask him whether or not, even with staff cuts of 84 people out of 370, the Canadian Wildlife Service could continue to perform its job. I think it is important to point out that the Government is under an obligation to Canadian people to try to be as effective as it can in the management of programs. We are facing a $34 billion deficit which we do not want to pass on to our children and grandchildren. It is important to find ways and means to make programs move effective. Obviously that overhead is crippling our economy. We must find ways and means to do things better. However, I will return to the question I asked of Mr. Brynaert as to whether the staff cuts and the budget cuts to the Canadian Wildlife Service could be lived with, assuming of course that perhaps in-house changes could be made to ensure that services would continue to be provided. But I might suggest that it is probable that the Department could operate with those kinds of cuts-providing some thought and planning had gone into where those cuts were made.
This group is profoundly affected by the cuts, yet its Executive Vice-President was quick to agree that government could live with cuts, probably these specific cuts, with some thought and planning on how they would be administered.
The Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker) was somewhat concerned about what the Executive Vice-President had said, and he questioned him on it. In reply Mr. Brynaert said:
1 am sure there are areas where there could be cuts, cuts that would not have dramatic effect in terms of carrying out the mandate and the responsibilities of the Department.
I should like to focus for a few minutes on one area of the Department and its responsibilities, that is, the Atmospheric Environment Service. We tend to overlook many of the functions which the Department has to carry out in its day to day operations. The weather affects all of us in a more dramatic way than we often think. Perhaps yesterday's storm was an example of how weather affects our daily lives. Because of the work of the Atmospheric Environment Service, yesterday's storm was forecast accurately and important decisions were made on transportation, snow removal, store and office closings and cancellation of public gatherings ahead of time so as to minimize the adverse effect of the weather on a variety of activities. It is the objective of that service to ensure that adequate information on the atmosphere, ice and sea is provided for. Their goal, of course, is the safety of lives, security of property, greater efficiency of a variety of economic activities and the maintenance and enhancement of environmental quality.
The Government feels that it can carry out this mandate with its policy of providing greater efficiency in government services. I would point out that new initiatives are being undertaken, as I mentioned in the reflection on the Estimates a few moments ago. In this area, a broad program to improve weather warnings on the West Coast for fishermen and other marine users has been implemented. The Government has moved aggressively to provide improved weather services for fishermen. Following the West Coast storm of October 12, 1984, a study was commissioned to determine the circumstances which led to the sinking of seven ships and the loss of five lives. The study was carried out by Professor LeBlond of the University of British Columbia. It was completed in December, 1984. The Government has now announced a series of responses to the LeBlond recommendations.
In December, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser) announced the number of weather observations taken by federal government vessels and that the recording of special observations for significant weather changes would be increased. He also indicated that co-ordination of fisheries openings and closings between the Weather Service and Fisheries vessels would be increased. In January, the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Blais-Grenier) announced an expansion of the West Coast committee which co-ordinates marine safety activities for roe herring fisheries to include the salmon fishery. She announced research into the causes for severe Pacific storms and the development of techniques to better forecast these events. She announced improvements of procedures to exchange weather observations and forecasts directly with the fishing fleet on a real time basis.
In February, the Government announced the establishment of a marine weather forecast position at the Pacific Weather Centre, giving specialized attention to providing marine weather forecasts and the introduction of a wave forecast service for two offshore areas and the acceleration of research and development on wave forecasting techniques for coastal areas in order to implement a comprehensive coastal service by 1987. It also announced improvements to the communications system between government services to provide more rapid exchange of weather information and to improve forecast services to the fishing community. These are just a few of the measures that have been undertaken, including automatic weather reporting services on the coast and in the coastal channels that will make life safer for our fishing and marine interests.
I would like to mention briefly climatic services. The climate program is very important to the Canadian Government, the

provinces and Territories. We have involvement from all those groups, plus universities in the private sector. Research is being carried out on the effects of increasing levels of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. This year, socio-economic impact studies are in process to gauge the probable effects of C02 induced climate changes on food, agriculture and on Great Lakes water resources.
On March 1, this Government announced a start of a one-year experiment which may eventually enable the Canadian public to obtain monthly and seasonal forecasts of climatic conditions on a regular basis. During the trial period, and I think this is interesting, selected organizations such as provincial Departments of Tourism, municipalities and fishery groups will be asked by Environment Canada to evaluate the format and usefulness of these experimental forecasts. Just imagine, if you will, in planning your holidays for this summer that you would be able to determine what the weather will be like in Prince Edward Island when you want to go there, and we welcome you all to our province.
In October of last year, Canadian astronaut Marc Garneau carried out successful experiments using the super sunphotom-eter aboard the U.S. space shuttle. The instrument was developed through joint efforts of the Atmospheric Environment Services Research Directorate and Canadian industry. It provides information supporting our continued research on climate as well as the stratospheric ozone layer and acid rain.
Over the past several months, this Government has provided additional funding for the completion of the report on the possible environmental effects of nuclear war. The study was completed by the Royal Society of Canada in early February. It describes the likely effects of a nuclear conflict on climatic conditions in Canada and around the world and, in particular, the so-called nuclear winter effect. The report is now being reviewed by Environment Canada and other federal Government Departments. I am pleased to announce on behalf of the Minister that she will be distributing to each and every Member of this House a copy of the report as soon as it can be printed so Members will have the opportunity to be apprised of the latest scientific assessment of this potential human and environmental catastrophe.
The demand for weather service continues to grow. It is widely used among government departments, federal and provincial, and in fact there were over 15 million contacts with the service in the last year. It certainly points out the need of providing this kind of service to the public.
Since 1976, the number of requests for information at the service has more than doubled. During that same period, staff members for the service have decreased by 10 per cent and expenditures remained nearly constant in real dollar terms. This productivity improvement has resulted from automation of AES operations such as the collection of wheather observation, preparation of forecasts, increased computerization of forecast methods and more rapid and widespread dissemination of products through an improved communication system. Obviously, the Government is providing better service and maintaining costs. In some areas, it was able to decrease costs

without imposing a further hardship on the Canadian taxpayer.
Improvements in the economies and the methods of delivering weather data and forecasts to the public have been achieved through a process of continuous review of staff deployment and technological improvements. In many cases, the service can be maintained at a lower level and still provide the objective of AES.
One way to improve efficiency, and I have already alluded to the fact that we can improve efficiency and productivity through automation, but one specific way that this has worked is the way in which AES has worked with high-tech companies in Canada. These companies have been able to build on the experience, and a number of them have a special but significant market niche for sophisticated scientific instrumentation which is now being sold in export markets. Because of the support of the Canadian Government, two of these high-tech companies building this equipment are now providing jobs to Canadian manufacturers who are selling this equipment abroad.
The Atmospheric Environment Service is responsible for the kind of weather reports and forecasts we hear daily. In fact, I would point out very quickly that they do provide in excess of
230.000	weather forecasts annually for 167 inland public forecast areas and all large population centres. They produce
130.000	marine weather warnings, advisories and forecasts annually for 101 marine regions. It produces 380,000 weather forecasts, amendments and warnings for 90 aviation areas and 170 airports. It also provides complete service for military operations.
There are some other things that the service provides which do not immediately come to mind, for instance, the long-range transport of air pollutants. AES provides the scientific leadership for the Canadian research effort concerned with the environmental impact of acid rain. In the area of toxic chemicals management, it looks at the persistent high concentration of toxic chemicals and how they would occur with increasing frequency over representative geographic areas. It provides scientific leadership in the areas of measurement, research and modelling.
Research on the following issues is also carried out: the danger to the earth's life-protecting stratospheric ozone layer which demands the use of certain chemicals, the effect of the build-up of atmospheric carbon dioxide caused by man's activities, even the effects of volcanic eruptions that may have long-lasting effects on man through climatic change and by significantly adding to the acidity of rain.
The National Weather Service, which I referred to, employs some 2,350 people from coast to coast and in remote Arctic locations, However, it enjoys the unselfish participation of twice as many unpaid volunteers who daily measure temperatures and precipitation for the National Climate Archives. That volunteer service is very important to this country as a whole.
