subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. It has been pointed out by several Members, and in particular the Hon. Member
March 5, 1985

for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) and the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton), that we are living in an age of very rapid industrial and technological change. One realizes that every year thousands of new chemical products are introduced in the market-place. Some of those products are foods, herbicides, pesticides and other chemical products. As well, different types of industrial practices occur. Different combinations of different chemicals are put together to produce a new product, or new types of by-products and industrial wastes, either in solid, liquid or gaseous form, are created.
In a highly industrial and technological society, there will be a very high rate of technological innovation. If we want to remain an industrial society, there is a technological imperative involved, that is, that we play a part in developing new products, chemicals and industrial practices in order that we remain competitive with other countries in the world. In fact, it is imperative to innovate continually in the industrial society.
Yet we know from past mistakes that in this rapidly changing industrial process mistakes do happen. Sometimes the mistakes can be fatal to the environment and to human health. That is why the state, as a social institution in a highly complex and industrial society, is so essential and important. It is the state which has the responsibility to ensure that no accidents occur, and that new products which are put on the market will not be harmful to human health or to the environment in present and future years.
The Government has a very special responsibility in an industrial society. It has a trust over our environment. It has to be a guardian over the quality of the land, the water and the air. It is a guardian for the present and for future generations. It is, therefore, with tremendous sadness that we see this newly elected Government, with its tremendous majority, decide to cut the Department of the Environment as one of its first acts. It is said that it has decided to cut from the Department some of the instruments which the Government needs in order to fulfil its role as the trustee of the environment. It is not only sad, it is shameful and it will not be forgiven by generations yet to come.
I would like to relate briefly some of the experiences I have had in the past in dealing with Liberal Governments. I would also like to refer to some of the chemical products which get on the market and the testing of those products for our health and safety. A number of years ago, when I was first elected, I became quite concerned with what was called the "IBT affair". "IBT" stands for International Biotest Laboratories in Illinois. This laboratory was the largest private toxicological laboratory in the world, I believe. It did the testing on just about all of the herbicides and pesticides on the market in Canada today and in fact in the United States as well. It did the tests to make certain that the use of these products would not cause cancer in the future and that, indeed, these products would be safe for the environment and for us as consumers.
Supply
It was discovered, Mr. Speaker, that this lab had deliberately falsified its tests. It had taken out dead rats and put in live rats. It had scratched out the results of its tests. A suit was filed in the United States, and several of the Chief officers of that company are now in jail. I brought this matter up in the House on numerous occasions. The Minister of National Health and Welfare at that time pooh-poohed me and said I was being sensationalist. The result was, Mr. Speaker, that the events in the United States, particularly in the courts, showed that I was not sensationalist.
Several of the products which IBT had tested had to be taken off the market. Governments, both in Canada and in the United States entered into an agreement to redo the testing of almost all the herbicides and pesticides on the market in Canada and the United States. But, Mr. Speaker, for a long period of time we had products on the market for which there was no accurate data proving that they were safe for human use and consumption. It became obvious at that time, Mr. Speaker, that the study of toxicology was essential in a modern contemporary industrialist society at a time when new chemicals were coming on the market at such a fast pace. It was not enough just to rely on the private sector to do those studies. Governments had to take this responsibility. It was recognized that it was a difficult field because there were very few trained toxicologists. It is an expensive field.
I as well as many others urged that an international public organization like the United Nations should become responsible for the toxicological studies which were needed to determine if all these new chemical products were safe to the environment, the users and the consumers. The establishment of a toxicology study centre in Canada was announced by the previous Government and was a truly important step. Unfortunately, we find that this Government has cut that proposal. We find that this Government now has cut the toxicological studies of the herring gulls. We find that the monitoring of of the effects on forests of the spraying of hundreds and thousands of pounds of toxic substances has been cut. We find that the program which monitored the effects of massive spraying of toxic materials on the Prairies has been cut. How unwise and how sad this is.
Previous studies, both in eastern Canada and in my home province, have shown that the poisons sprayed-and, indeed, herbicides and pesticides are poisons-collected through ground water into lakes and gullies is having a detrimental effect on the life chain. Studies have shown that at the base of the life chain are microscopic organisms which generally exist in the mud and the bottom of gullies and lakes, and there is an unacceptable high rate of deformities among these lower life forms in the life chain. These lower levels form food for fish, and fish form the food for the birds and for human beings. So, Mr. Speaker, these toxic substances are moving up into the life chain. That is why it is so important to have monitoring in place. Monitoring provides an early warning system to human beings. The destruction of the program, Mr. Speaker, which gives us that early monitoring system is irresponsible. It is stupidity to the highest degree, and we will pay the price in the

March 5, 1985
Supply
future. The few million dollars that the Government will save today, it will have to repay in hundreds of millions of dollars in the future as the toxic substances move up the life chain. How stupid is this action of the Government! How stupid it is to save a few millions today which it will have to repay a hundredfold in the future!
We know of the effect of thalidamide. We know of the heartaches and human suffering which that drug caused to untold numbers of people. What the Government is doing with this action is disabling the country from preventing the type of catastrophe like thalidamide.
In my own home Province of Saskatchewan, we know that there is some correlation between the number of miscarriages which occur after crop spraying time. This hard to put a correct statistical correlation on it, Mr. Speaker, because there are too many variables still involved, such as wind patterns. We know that the chemical spray is concentrated in certain urban areas. But I think it is fair to say that those who are knowledgeable in the field know that the chances for miscarriages increase because of crop spraying. Is it any wonder? Logic would tell you that. Obviously when hundreds and thousands of pounds of toxic substances are sprayed in the air, substances which are meant to kill weeds and insects, it can also have a detrimental effect on human health. So when the Government makes these cuts, it does a tremendous disservice to the present generation and generations to come.
There is also concern about the future, Mr. Speaker. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency issued an amazing report around a year and a half ago. It warned that about 15 to 20 years from now we will begin to see the greenhouse effect. It predicts that this effect will have a tremendous environmental impact of a global nature. It warns that the build-up of carbon particles in the atmosphere will create a tremendous climatic change around our world, and we will begin to see it in our lifetime. That, Mr. Speaker, is just an amazing warning from an institution like the EPA, an agency which would not unduly alarm American citizens because of some false or whimsy reports. It was a well researched warning. Yet when we see the cuts this Government has introduced in the Department of the Environment, we begin to realize that the Government is not really concerned about the future. It is not concerned about things like the greenhouse effect; if it is 15 or 20 years away, forget it. This Government is only concerned about four-year terms. But environmental concerns are not just for four-year or eight-year terms but much longer terms. Private industry does not have those because the concern of private industry is the profit margin and the bottom line. Whether you like it or not, that is the nature of private enterprise. But Government should have a long-term concern, because if it does not, who in heaven's name in our world, in our society, has that concern? No one. It is the duty of the Government to become concerned, not just about this year or next year, this term or next term. This institution is the only one with the responsibility not for this generation alone but for generations to come. We are the guardians of our environment. We are the guardians of our world, and the cut-backs this Government has introduced mean giving up that guardianship. That is inexcusable.
One begins to wonder the reason for this. I mean, normally I tend to get along with the Conservatives; not the new right in the United States, they frighten the heck out of me but the traditional small "c" conservatives who think in terms of conserving, preserving and husbanding our resources. They have been critical of past Liberal Governments for squandering our resources and the environment for the sake of development for now and the heck with the future. I have always felt a very close affinity with those small "c" conservatives who believe in conserving. We have to conserve our resources, our environment, our energy, our fresh water and our air. We have to conserve these precious commodities because they are not inexhaustible. We are living not in an infinite world but in a very finite world. But now we see those very Conservatives are now destroying their own philosophy by cutting back on the Department of the Environment.
Why are they doing it? I see a pattern in the cut-backs in the Department of the Environment and in the NRC. Where are the cut-backs in the NRC? Are there cut-backs in Atomic Energy research? Oh, no. Are they in alternative energy? Oh, yes. Where are the cut-backs in the grants to oil companies? Oh, no, don't touch them. But there are cut-backs in developing alternative energy sources and home insulation. Everything that would help conserve and preserve is being cut back. I am afraid that the pattern is clear, Mr. Speaker. This Government here is not for the long term but for the good times.

It is here to rape and to plunder the resources now and forget about the future. It is a Government which is for freeing things up for unfettered private enterprise. "Put away the silly environmental restrictions. We do not want to hear about deformities in herring gull eggs. We do not want to hear about deformities in primitive life forms at the bottom of our lakes. We do not want any of this early warning system. Well, Mr. Speaker, this tremendous irresponsibility, this stupidity that we will pay for many times over in the future, this is why I stand here in support of the motion of non-confidence. I hope and urge all Members of this House to vote according to their conscience and not according to their political affiliation and loyalties. It is the future of this country, its environment, its precious natural environment, and generations to come which are at stake.

DDT in Lake Ontario were causing the gulls to disappear. However, he will also know that problem seems to have been solved in that the gull population has certainly expanded and seems to be in hand. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, using the Member's logic, we would never have had the program to begin with because there was not a problem to begin with. We instituted the program as an early warning system. When the problem started we were able to pick up on it.
I cannot agree with the Hon. Member when he says the problem is gone. Two years ago I, along with several of my colleagues, visited the Love Canal and Hyde Park dump sites. At the Hyde Park dump site there are hundreds of thousands of pounds of dioxin. Let me explain to the Hon. Member that one ten-thousandth of a part of dioxin, that is a little speck that you see in the sunlight on a dusty day, is enough to cause cancer and kill a person. At the Hyde Park dump site in Niagara there are over 100,000 pounds of dioxin stored. We know from the past that there has been leaching from that dump site through the Niagara River into the Great Lakes. They have found dioxins along the Niagara River. In fact, it would be a tremendous terrorist plot, if one were to write a terrorist novel, for someone to blow up some of those makeshift dams which exist around the Hyde Park dump site during a period of heavy rains. The Hyde Park dump site is a ticking time bomb. There is leaching of dioxins out of that site into the Great Lakes system.
We need the monitoring system as an early warning for us all. Not until those dump sites of sewage and industrial wastes around the Great Lakes have been cleared up should the early warning system be dismantled. As long as those dangers continue to exist, we must keep the monitoring system. To destroy that monitoring system is to pluck out your eyes. That is how dumb and stupid it is.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that the Member does not know what is happening. The herring gull program has only been reduced from six people knocking open herring gull eggs to one person. Must we continue forever doing the same old thing without getting at the new problems in the environment as they develop?

I am dismayed to hear the Hon. Member say that the six people were only cracking open eggs. The Hon. Member is dealing with a very serious problem.
They have not killed the program; there is still one person left, he states. I understand that if the one person who is left in the program observes deformities in the eggs and offsprings, he cannot even report them. The Government does not want to hear any of that stuff because it disturbs people. It means that local people get upset, form committees, and demand more regulations on industry. The Government does not want more regulations on industry, so it shuts down the programs which supply the information that gets people all upset. The Government would rather have the people accept what is going down and not know and understand the dangers that exist to their health and safety. That is the attitude of the Government and of the Hon. Member and it is deplorable.

I am getting the impression from the Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong) that today is the first day of the last days of our lives, that the world is ending, but indeed it is not. The Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker) referred to the word "impossible". Napoleon said that the word "impossible" exists only in the dictionary. The former Government, however, left us with trying to do the impossible in this country.
The financial corporate community of Canada has been saying that we did not go far enough on November 8. Many respected research organizations in the country, such as the Business Council on National Issues, the Conference Board of Canada and the C.D. Howe Institute, are saying that we did not go far enough with our cuts. They are saying that we cannot continue to live beyond our means in this country. The Member for Regina East spoke about cuts across the board. He spoke about all the Ministries and gave us a litany, as did many other Members this afternoon, of cuts. Does the

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I understand that the PMO has increased its budget by 50 some per cent. I think most Canadians would rather have seen that money spent on wildlife and to protect the health and safety of our environment and water quality than to increase the propaganda arm of the Prime Minister's Office. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to contribute to this debate by speaking about renewable energy, and in particular about research into renewable energy. I would like to speak about the serious questions that the cuts at the National Research Council energy division have raised about our ability to cope with the depletion of conventional energy resources, and the relationship of these cuts to the protection and management of the environment.
We live in a complex world, Mr. Speaker, and the decisions we make sometimes have consequences which we cannot foresee. Earlier today I asked the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Siddon) whether he was aware of the consequences of his decision to cut research spending on Canadian aid programs in Africa at the time that he made the decision. In answer to me he said that there is quite a distance between the cuts in basic research and the problems of starving millions in Africa.
I would suggest that it is not so, Mr. Speaker. I would suggest that there is indeed a very direct relationship. On November 8, we had the elimination of the research program in renewable energy. In January, the National Research Council informed CIDA that it could no longer provide the research support for the programs that it had contemplated to provide for irrigation using Canadian technology in the desert. In February, CIDA responded by indefinitely postponing its program because this research support was not available. These connections may be hard for people to see.
I would like to suggest to the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Siddon) and to his Cabinet colleagues that research is not conducted in a vacuum. Indeed, technology has application in many areas.
It is precisely the applications of this technology and the long-term consequences of the use of technology that we expect the Government to be studying when it makes decisions of this nature.
Let me review briefly the history of Canada's renewable energy. It was born out of the oil crisis in the mid and late 1970s. In the National Energy Program, the Government foresaw a greater role for alternative and renewable energy in Canada. I quote from an excerpt of the program:
The realities of the energy future indicate the wisdom of accelerated efforts to develop new and renewable energy forms-
This program was followed by the House of Commons special committee on alternative energy and oil substitution which studied this subject for one year. It took a half century perspective-I do not suggest that a half century perspective is too long-on Canadian energy development and presented some 65 recommendations to foster the introduction of alternative energy sources, technologies and fuels into our energy system.
Considering the variety of concerns including the depletion of conventional energy resources, environmental impact, regional energy disparity, strategic considerations, diversity in energy supply and social benefits, this committee argued that the twenty-first century would see a profound change in Canada's energy system away from hydrocarbons and toward sustainable resources. Support programs were gradually developed by the Government and an interdepartmental panel on energy research and development was established to co-ordinate the Government efforts in the areas of renewable energy, conservation, fossil fuels, new liquid fuels, conventional energy and nuclear energy. In 1983 and 1984, some $54 million was provided for the research programs operated by the NRC Division of Energy. The following programs accounted for some $41 million of research expenditures: heat pumps, fusion energy, solar energy, bioenergy, wind energy, hydrogen and energy storage. It should be noted that some three-quarters of this research was conducted by the private sector under contracts with the National Research Council. It is these programs and indeed the entire NRC Energy Division that were cancelled by the Government last November 8.
[Translation)
The renewable energy industry consists largely of small- and medium-sized businesses, many of which have been in existence for only ten years or less. Today, some of these companies are financially dependent on public research programs such as the one initiated by the National Research Council. About 500 companies are directly active in research, design, manufacturing, distribution and installation of various lines of products in the renewable energy field. About 225 companies are manufacturers who in 1984 employed about 5,000 people and had sales of nearly $530 million, $30 million of which to export markets. These companies offer products that have been quick to acquire an international reputation. Our future for exports looks promising, provided we can remain competitive at the international level. We export mainly to the United States but also to Africa, Central America, South America and Asia.
According to a study carried out in 1983 by Frost and Sullivan, a consulting firm, international sales of biomass-based products, photovoltaic cells, small hydroelectric turbines, windmills and solar-thermal technology are now estimated at $3.5 billion and are expected to reach $15 billion by 1990.
March 5, 1985



It is against this background that we learned on November 8 of the complete elimination of the NRC Division of Energy. The reaction from the industry can only be characterized as disbelief. Research contracts which had been approved and were about to be signed were cancelled. Firms which had been counting on contracts were forced to lay off personnel and cancel projects. In spite of the grand promises of the Government, there was no warning, no consultation and no alternative presented by the Government.
The reaction from the industry was predictable. It is perhaps instructive for Tory Members in the House to hear some of that reaction. From Vancouver, a Mr. P. William Bishop wrote to the Minister of Science and Technology on November 24. He said:
From this distance, the decision to cut the entire NRC Energy Division seems somewhat arbitrary. I am concerned that in your keenness to make cuts you may not have fully considered the impact on the private sector.
Mr. Bishop went on to refer to the superwindow program and the plasma lamp.
Cutting the research at this stage will in my opinion be an act of vandalism ... cutting back on private sector research in Vancouver is not why I have supported the Tory party for years.

Here is what Societe d'energie solaire du Canada Inc. Director Jacques Beaudet wrote in his letter of November 29 to the Hon. Member for Dollard:
For over ten years now, Canadians have made a lot of efforts and spent their own money to promote science, technology and the use of new energy sources. Government policies have helped put Canada's experts on the international scene ... It would be a shame if a hasty decision, perhaps inspired by short-term objectives, were to make Canadians lose all the benefits of work already done and supported by Government policies.

Let me quote one other comment from the industry. Michael Bein of Chelsea, Quebec, wrote the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) on December 18:
I am all for getting rid of waste in government and reducing Canada's enormous budget deficit... but why use a chain saw when a scalpel, or at least a butcher's knife, will do?
Canada's fledgling solar industry stands to be wiped out, with something like 2000 private sector jobs lost, and with areas where we had a chance to be the world leader handed over to the Japanese on a silver platter. I am especially surprised that a Tory government would condone such an attack on small business.
It is hard to fathom why this particular decision was made. There was many questions that have been raised and very few answers offered by the Government. Last November 13, the Minister of State for Science and Technology said that this program was the least essential of all the activities of the National Research Council. We have no indication on what basis that determination was made. Obviously, many people in industry do not agree with him.
He also said on November 29 that the Government was:
-not sufficiently convinced of progress to the extent that special allocated funding should be continued in this area. Alternate energy could obtain funding for its projects through EMR and other government agencies. If proponents of
Supply
projects in the solar energy industry wish to come forward, their application would be considered alongside that of anyone else's.
He did not indicate any consideration of the effect of this decision on jobs, Canada's export potential, on regional development or on the environment.
Another question which comes to mind is why the Division of Energy was not consulted. On November 19, the Secretary General of the National Research Council was reported as saying that the decision about what program cuts would be made to fulfil the budget reduction were made by the Government, not the agency.
Another question I have is, why was this entire division eliminated rather than the reduction spread throughout the NRC? Savings in 1985-1986 are forecast to be some $32 million. The NRC last year had an over-all budget of $502 million. Why not cut back all programs by 5 per cent or 6 per cent and preserve this particular program?
Were other alternatives considered, such as cutting a small percentage of expenditures in non-renewable energy and thereby providing funds to preserve a smaller Division of Energy? There is no indication that that was considered.
The Tory Government says it favours small business. Why harm an industry made up of small businesses? As I indicated earlier, 75 per cent of the research managed by the National Research Council is contracted out to the private sector. What about the Wright report which recently studied all aspects of government research and development? It recommended that greater efforts should be made by federal labs to work with industry by means of contracting out and that due recognition should be given to scientists and administrators supporting these efforts. Why, therefore, cut a program which corresponds precisely to this recommendation, which presumably is supported by the Government? I would ask you, Mr. Speaker, to compare the cost of this program, again some $50 million, and its benefits to other forms of government support for the oil and gas industry or, let us say, to the cost of cleaning up polluting industry. The folly of this decision becomes all the more remarkable: $54 million, the 1983-84 budget of the Division of Energy, as opposed to billions of dollars that are spent on loan guarantees, PIP grants and subsidies to the oil and gas industry; $54 million as opposed to billions that must be spent to clean up acid rain. The Globe and Mail in an article on February 16 reported that Canada's major nickel and copper smelter operators may have to spend over $ 1 billion on capital equipment to clean the air.
There is no comparison whatsoever between the $54 million, the amount is almost picayune, that was invested in a promising young industry, as compared to the billions of dollars spent on more mature industry in this country.
It is not just a matter of cost, Mr. Speaker; electricity exports to the U.S. are threatened. The National Governors Association made up of Governors from 50 U.S. states resolved last year to press for legislation that would prevent

March 5, 1985
Supply
U.S. imports of Canadian electricity unless Canada reduced its emissions that cause acid rain.
I would like to conclude my comments by saying that nothing other than the complete restoration of this budget would put this industry on sound footing. Our Party is also concerned about the deficit. However, when we look at this program and we see its relationship to the future of a promising industry in our country and when we compare the levels of support that are accorded renewable energy in many other countries, there is no foundation for this decision.
There has been much talk this afternoon about efficiency, about the necessity, the mandate this Government received, to control the deficit. That is true, Mr. Speaker, but there is another part to that. There is the part that says the Government must act responsibly, that its decisions must be made, as we have heard so often in the past few days, in the best interests of this country. The Minister of State for Science and Technology earlier today indicated that he did not see the connection between basic research and the problems of feeding starving millions in Africa. I would suggest that this is a totally irresponsible way to address the long-term consequences of research and development. I would suggest that the Minister of State for Science and Technology, if he has not done so already, meet with the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Blais-Grenier) and with other Cabinet colleagues and discuss some of the long-term consequences. The only conclusion that one can come to is that this Government, as has been suggested this afternoon, is only concerned with the shortterm. Its only preoccupation is with the next election.
Future generations of Canadians depend on our Government to act in a more responsible manner when it comes to a crucial issue such as our environment and research spending as it affects the environment.
